UEFA votes to boycott World Cup over FIFA stake sale plans
item.description:
UEFA and its 55 European member nations voted unanimously on Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all FIFA tournaments in protest at world football's governing body's plan to sell a stake to external investors.

The dramatic move came after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) issued a scathing letter to the continent's 47 member associations and warned the proposal would never succeed without the support of all of football's regional blocs.

"UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one. We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors," UEFA said in a statement.

"As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership."

European football's ruling body said the World Cup was not for sale and could not be treated as an investment product or surrendered to private investors.

UEFAThe moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever

"This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA’s duty as the custodian of world football," it said of the proposal.

"The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure."

AFC expresses deep concern

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa said his body was not consulted by FIFA at any level prior to the public announcement and declared that, and the lack of any detailed governance, financial or legal analysis of the proposal, as "totally unacceptable".

"FIFA’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of Continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency," added the Bahraini.

The AFC's forthright criticism heaps further pressure on FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has spearheaded the contentious plan to create a US$20 billion subsidiary to run the World Cup and its other events, while offering minority stakes to private investors.

CONCACAF, the regional bloc for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, also criticised FIFA for a lack of consultation.

Infantino offered FIFA's 211 member associations US$40 million each if they agree to the proposal by 19 September as part of a US$10 billion package to become available from 1 January, 2027.

If rejected, the package would revert to US$2.7 billion previously offered, around $10 million per member association.

Infantino said FIFA will put the proposal to a vote by its member associations (MAs) and then to its executive Council.

However, Sheikh Salman said it would need all six of the regional blocs behind it.

"Such an initiative will not succeed without the support of all the confederations, which is not the case now," he wrote.

The African confederation's executive committee will meet next week to evaluate the proposal, while the Oceania confederation, the smallest regional bloc with 11 full member nations, said it would discuss the proposal at a meeting next month.

South American governing body CONMEBOL has yet to comment publicly.

'Tournaments should not be sale'

Players' bodies have also expressed opposition to FIFA's plan, with FIFPRO, the global players union, warning the proposal would irreversibly reshape the incentives underpinning the competitions in which players work and build careers.

Australia's players union joined the criticism on Thursday, saying the governing body was putting pressure on member associations to wave the proposal through while sidelining the athletes and fans who generate the value of the tournaments.

"The PFA is disturbed by the lack of transparency surrounding the proposal and the absence of meaningful consultation with those that generate the value that FIFA is seeking to exploit - the players and the fans," Professional Footballers Australia said in a statement.

"At a time when football desperately requires greater transparency, accountability and good governance, proposals of this significance raise questions about who the game is run by and in whose interests. These tournaments should not be for sale."

Former Liberty Media Chief Executive Greg Maffei, a commercial adviser to FIFA on the project, said it was not a matter of "selling the World Cup” and the governing body would always have majority control.

"There’s a trend of this going on in sports all over the place,” the American, who oversaw Liberty Media'a acquisition of Formula One's commercial rights in 2017, told the Financial Times. “It’s something that all sorts of people have done.”

item.title: DU suspends Sadeka Halim, 2 others, forms panel to review AL-era recruitments
item.description:
Dhaka University has temporarily suspended three faculty members, including Professor Sadeka Halim of the Department of Sociology, over separate allegations.

The university has also decided to relieve four other teachers of their academic and administrative responsibilities.

The decisions were taken at a meeting of the university's Syndicate on 28 July, chaired by Vice-Chancellor Professor ABM Obaidul Islam, according to a press release issued on Thursday.

The press release said Professor Sadeka Halim, a former VC of Jagannath University, was temporarily suspended from her position at Dhaka University over allegations including conduct unbecoming of a teacher inside and outside the classroom, moral misconduct, and other complaints.

Based on complaints from students of different batches and the findings of an inquiry committee, Professor Md Shafiqul Islam and Professor Afroza Shelly of the Department of Nuclear Engineering were also temporarily suspended.

The Syndicate also decided to remove Professor Md Abdul Muhit of the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology from his position as department chairman and relieve him of all academic and administrative duties.

According to the press release, the action was taken over allegations of activities contrary to the spirit of the July mass uprising, spreading propaganda against the university administration and the government, and supporting and issuing threats on behalf of a banned organisation.

On the same allegations, Professor Abu Sara Shamsur Rauf of the Department of Pharmaceutical Technology and Professor Md Rafiqul Islam (Rafiq Shahriar) of the Department of Peace and Conflict Studies were also relieved of all academic and administrative responsibilities.

The press release further stated that Professor Mohammad Bahauddin of the Department of Persian Language and Literature was relieved of his academic and administrative duties over allegations of various irregularities in the department and plagiarism involving similarities between MPhil and PhD theses.

In a separate decision, AKM Mahbub Mustafa, supervising engineer (civil) at the Office of the Chief Engineer, was temporarily suspended from his job for activities deemed contrary to office discipline.

Committee formed to review 15 years of recruitment

The Syndicate also formed a committee to review all alleged irregularities in recruitment at Dhaka University between 1 January 2009 and June 2024 and assess the transparency of the appointment process.

The committee will be headed by Pro-VC (academic) Professor Abdus Salam, with the deans of all university faculties serving as members.

Another committee, led by Pro-VC (administration) Professor Mohammad Al-Mujaddedi Al-Feshani, was formed to review research activities conducted under the Higher Education Quality Enhancement Project (HEQEP), funded by the World Bank and the University Grants Commission (UGC), during the same period. The committee will also examine whether research project funds were used appropriately.

The press release added that the Syndicate decided to take action against individuals, groups and organisations allegedly involved in activities deemed contrary to the spirit of the July mass uprising. It said further decisions would be taken after a verification process.

The meeting also approved the construction of a "July Memorial Monument" on the plaza adjacent to the university's Administrative Building in memory of those killed during the July mass uprising. The foundation stone for the monument is scheduled to be laid on 5 August.

item.title: Many progresses made: Trump's special envoy after meeting foreign minister
item.description:
In Dhaka, US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor has met with Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman.

Officials concerned have indicated that discussions were held on strengthening bilateral cooperation between the United States and Bangladesh.

Sergio Gor arrived in Dhaka today, Thursday afternoon for a three-day visit.

In the evening, he met with the Foreign Minister at the state guest house Padma.

Trump's special envoy Sergio Gor will arrive in Dhaka today

Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that after 6pm, the Foreign Minister and the US special envoy sat down for a meeting with their representatives.

Later, Sergio Gor had a private conversation with Khalilur Rahman for about 20 minutes.

American billionaire Sergio Gor is serving as the US ambassador to India.

Along with this, Trump appointed him as the special envoy for South and Central Asia. This is his first visit to Bangladesh after taking on the role of US ambassador in New Delhi last January.

After the meeting with the Foreign Minister, Sergio Gor wrote in a post on social media platform X, ''I am pleased to have met with Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman on my first visit to Bangladesh and discuss working together to strengthen US -Bangladesh bilateral relations. Many positive progresses have occurred.''

Since the BNP government assumed office last February, Sergio Gor has become the third senior US official to visit Dhaka from Washington. Earlier in March, Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asia Paul Kapur and in May, Deputy Assistant US Trade Representative for South and Central Asia Brendan Lynch visited Bangladesh.

After Sergio Gor's arrival in Dhaka in the afternoon, US Ambassador Brent T Christensen expressed his happiness in a post on the verified Facebook page of the US Embassy in Bangladesh, saying, ''I am delighted to welcome my friend, US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor, to Bangladesh. His visit will further strengthen the strategic partnership, regional security, and economic cooperation between the US and Bangladesh.''

Trump’s special envoy due in Dhaka to sound out Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction

According to diplomatic sources, during Sergio Gor's ongoing visit, discussions on Bangladesh's current foreign policy priorities, regional strategic positioning, and the future of Dhaka-Washington relations will be highlighted.

Especially in the context of increased international interest following the Prime Minister's visit to China in June, the Foreign Minister's visit to Moscow in the same month, and the Turkish Foreign Minister's visit to Dhaka, Washington's evaluation may be reflected in this visit. If necessary, he may convey messages from President Donald Trump's administration to Bangladesh's leadership.

Diplomatic sources have indicated that tomorrow, Friday, US Envoy Sergio Gor will visit Cox's Bazar to inspect the situation of Rohingya refugees on the ground. On the last day of the visit, Saturday, he will meet with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

Digital Democracy Initiative convenes National Advocacy Event on Digital Democracy
item.description:
Accountability Lab, in collaboration with Kashful Foundation, successfully organised the National Advocacy Event on Digital Democracy under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) South Asia at Hotel Sarina, Dhaka, reports a press release.

The event brought together policymakers, government officials, development partners, academics, media professionals, civil society representatives, digital rights advocates, and youth leaders to discuss the future of digital democracy in Bangladesh and explore pathways for building a safer, more inclusive, and participatory digital society.

The event commenced with welcome remarks by Monjurul Alam, country programme officer of the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) at Accountability Lab, who highlighted the importance of youth participation and multi-stakeholder collaboration in strengthening democratic values in the digital age.

The chief guest, Md Taibur Rahman, director general of the National Cyber Security Agency (NCSA), shared the Government of Bangladesh's ongoing initiatives to strengthen digital governance, cybersecurity, public service delivery, and digital infrastructure.

He emphasized the importance of digital awareness, community-based fact-checking, and stronger partnerships among government institutions, civil society, media, academia, and young people to address emerging digital challenges.

He stated, "The Government is ready to partner with civil society and youth to empower digital democracy in Bangladesh."

The keynote address, titled ‘The Next Generation of Democracy: Digital Rights, Youth Advocacy, and Policy Reform in Bangladesh’, was delivered by Professor Sarfaraj Hamid, dean of the Faculty of Law at Bangladesh University of Business and Technology (BUBT).

He described digital rights as an extension of fundamental human rights and highlighted the importance of privacy, freedom of expression, data protection, accountability, and inclusive policymaking in the digital era.

Reflecting on recent experiences of internet restrictions and the growing influence of digital technologies, he encouraged young people to play an active role in shaping rights-based digital policies and strengthening democratic participation.

The first panel discussion, ‘Shaping Inclusive Digital Futures: Civic Rights, Democratic Participation, and Diverse Voices in the 21st Century’, showcased experiences and innovations developed by Digital Democracy Initiative South Asia sub-grantee organizations in Bangladesh.

The discussion highlighted practical approaches to strengthening digital democracy through digital literacy, community-based fact-checking, civic technology, youth leadership, and digital safety initiatives.

Speakers emphasized that empowering communities with digital knowledge and promoting inclusive participation are essential for addressing misinformation, online violence, and unequal access to digital spaces.

The second panel discussion, ‘Youth at the Heart of Digital Democracy: Building an Inclusive Civic Ecosystem in Bangladesh’, focused on the evolving role of young people in promoting responsible digital citizenship and democratic engagement.

Discussions explored freedom of expression, cyber awareness, digital inclusion, media accountability, gender-sensitive reporting, cyberbullying, and ethical technology use.

Panelists encouraged young people to become informed and responsible digital citizens by promoting truthful information, respectful dialogue, and active civic participation while standing against online harassment and digital injustice.

Throughout the event, speakers emphasised that protecting digital democracy requires collective responsibility. They underscored the need to strengthen media and information literacy, improve digital awareness, enhance legal and institutional frameworks, support community-led fact-checking initiatives, and ensure meaningful youth participation in policymaking.

The event concluded with a renewed commitment from government institutions, civil society organizations, development partners, media, academia, and youth leaders to strengthen collaboration and continue advancing digital rights, transparency, accountability, and inclusive civic engagement in Bangladesh's evolving digital landscape.

US actor and singer Jared Leto on Wednesday denied allegations of sexual assault and harassment leveled against him by ten women in a new documentary aired by the BBC.

The women said they were victimised by Leto between 2002 and 2016.

Two of them accused him of sexual assault when they were 17 years old, while another said the actor threatened her with sexual assault when she was 19.

Four other women described sexual harassment during phone calls from the lead singer of the rock band Thirty Seconds to Mars.

"I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life," the 54-year-old actor said in a statement. "These claims are absolutely and categorically false."

Actor who accused Spacey says was 'frozen' during alleged 1980s assault

The actor, who won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar in 2014 for "Dallas Buyers Club," has faced such accusations before.

item.title: Khalilur: Bangladesh-US ties moving in positive direction
item.description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman has said Bangladesh’s relations with the United States are moving in a “very positive direction” as the two countries seek to further deepen cooperation in trade, investment, energy, migration and regional issues.
“Our bilateral relationship is now moving in a very positive direction and we expect it to progress further in the coming days,” he told journalists after a meeting with visiting US President’s Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Ambassador Sergio Gor at the state guest house Padma in the capital.
Prime Minister’s Adviser on Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir also attended the meeting held at the foreign ministry.
The foreign minister said the discussions reflected the growing momentum in Bangladesh-US relations and focused on ways to further strengthen the longstanding partnership.
“We had a very productive discussion. Bangladesh and the United States currently enjoy an excellent bilateral relationship, and we discussed how to take it forward,” he said.
Referring to his recent engagements with senior US officials in Manila, Rahman said he had met Ambassador Gor earlier on the sidelines of the Asean meetings and also held talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
He said today’s meeting covered a broad range of bilateral issues, including trade, investment, energy cooperation and migration.
“Given the nature of the meeting, we discussed these issues in broad terms rather than in detail,” he said.
The foreign minister said no discussion took place regarding Bangladesh’s relations with China or India, adding that he saw no indication of US concern on those issues.
On energy cooperation, Rahman said Bangladesh and the United States already have an energy memorandum of understanding, while Dhaka continues to seek cooperation from various countries to address its energy needs.
Replying to a question on Bangladesh’s aviation sector, he said the government had informed the US side that, besides Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ fleet expansion program, a Bangladeshi private airline had recently placed a significant order for Boeing aircraft, reflecting the country’s growing aviation industry.
On the Rohingya crisis, the foreign minister said the United States remains Bangladesh’s largest humanitarian partner, providing more than half of the international assistance for the displaced Myanmar nationals sheltered in Bangladesh.
He said both sides discussed maintaining international pressure on Myanmar and expressed hope that continued US support would contribute to efforts for a sustainable solution to the crisis.
Rahman also dismissed reports suggesting that the United States had proposed a humanitarian corridor into Myanmar.
“No such proposal was made. There was no discussion from the US side regarding any humanitarian corridor,” he said.
Responding to a question on US tariffs, the foreign minister said Bangladesh had been placed in the 10% tariff category following the completion of investigations under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, while some countries were subjected to higher rates.
He said Bangladesh had also secured an important concession under a tariff quota arrangement that would provide greater market access for garments manufactured using American cotton or US-made man-made fibres.
“That is a significant achievement which has received little attention,” he said.
The foreign minister said Bangladesh had also continued discussions with the United States on the withdrawal of sanctions imposed on the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB), describing the matter as an ongoing process.
Rahman said the meeting also included discussions on his forthcoming assumption of office as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on September 8.
He said it was natural for the United States, as one of the principal architects of the United Nations, to maintain close engagement with the incoming president of the General Assembly.
Asked about emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, Rahman said the global landscape was evolving rapidly, with competing technological systems taking shape, and discussions on such issues would continue as international positions become clearer.

item.title: Luxury cars, fake stickers fuel new wave of Yaba trafficking in Cox's Bazar
item.description:
Yaba traffickers along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border have adopted increasingly sophisticated methods, using luxury vehicles, counterfeit government and military stickers, hidden compartments and fake identities to transport large consignments of the narcotic across the country, prompting heightened concern among law enforcement agencies.
Authorities say overland trafficking through Cox's Bazar has regained momentum after a temporary shift to maritime routes, with private cars and high-end SUVs now emerging as preferred carriers for large shipments.
Recent operations by police, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and the Department of Narcotics Control (DNC) reveal a growing pattern of traffickers disguising their vehicles with fake stickers of the Bangladesh Army, government ministries, lawyers, media organisations and political parties to avoid scrutiny at checkpoints.
The latest seizure came on July 27, when BGB personnel at the Hwaikyong checkpoint in Teknaf intercepted a luxury private car carrying 106,000 Yaba tablets. One suspect, Saiful Islam Khokon of PM Khali in Cox's Bazar Sadar, was arrested.
Officials said several major consignments have been intercepted in Cox's Bazar, Ramu and Ukhiya during July, highlighting the resurgence of organised cross-border trafficking networks.
One of the most significant incidents occurred on July 24, when police recovered 28,000 Yaba tablets from a Toyota Land Cruiser displaying a fake Bangladesh Army sticker near Cox's Bazar Central Bus Terminal. The tablets had been concealed inside a specially built compartment beneath the vehicle's seats.
The driver, retired army member Obaidul Hasan, was arrested after allegedly attempting to flee. Police said they were investigating whether the operation was linked to a larger trafficking syndicate.
A day earlier, BGB members seized 10,685 Yaba tablets hidden inside a specially modified engine compartment of a private car travelling from Teknaf to Chattogram. The driver, Md Farid of Rangunia, reportedly admitted transporting the drugs.
Earlier this month, police recovered 30,000 Yaba tablets concealed inside a modified CNG cylinder of an unregistered private car at Himchhari on the Marine Drive road. Investigators said the cylinder had been converted into a secret chamber designed to evade routine inspections.
In another operation, DNC officials seized 6,000 Yaba tablets from a private car bearing counterfeit stickers of the Ministry of Home Affairs and Mirpur DOHS. Three suspects, including two women, were arrested. Investigators believe the group was posing as tourists to reduce suspicion at security checkpoints.
Law enforcement officials said traffickers are constantly changing their methods, using concealed compartments in seats, engine bays, air-conditioning panels and gas cylinders. Women, children and tourists are also being used as cover to minimise suspicion during roadside inspections.
Authorities also expressed concern over the widespread misuse of counterfeit official stickers. They noted that fake logos of government agencies, the military, the judiciary and media organisations can be reproduced easily at commercial printing shops, while the absence of a digital verification system at checkpoints makes immediate authentication difficult.
Cox's Bazar Sadar Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Sheikh Mohammad Ali said the misuse of official insignia to facilitate drug trafficking was a serious matter.
"We are investigating whether organised criminal networks are behind these incidents," he said.
DNC Cox's Bazar Deputy Director Somen Mondal said traffickers were increasingly relying on private vehicles and fake government identities.
"Intelligence surveillance has been strengthened, and inspections at key checkpoints have been intensified," he said.
Lieutenant Colonel Zahirul Islam, commanding officer of BGB's Ukhiya Battalion (64 BGB), said security forces were maintaining strict surveillance on suspicious vehicles following the recent increase in luxury car-based smuggling.
Legal experts said traffickers transporting commercial quantities of narcotics through specially modified vehicles could face the death penalty or life imprisonment under the Narcotics Control Act, 2018 (amended in 2023), while those using counterfeit government insignia could also be prosecuted under the Penal Code for forgery, personation and fraud.
Local residents and anti-drug campaigners have urged authorities to install X-ray scanners on major highways and introduce a nationwide digital verification system for official vehicle stickers and registration details, arguing that conventional roadside searches alone are no longer sufficient to combat increasingly sophisticated trafficking networks.

item.title: Sergio Gor: Lots of positive developments in Bangladesh-US ties
item.description:
US Special Envoy on South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on Thursday said there had been "lots of positive developments" in Bangladesh-US relations after holding talks with Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman.
"It was great to meet Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman during my first visit to Bangladesh and discuss working together to strengthen the US-Bangladesh relationship. Lots of positive developments," Gor wrote on X after the meeting at the State Guest House Padma.
Prime Minister's Foreign Affairs Adviser Humaiun Kobir and US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T Christensen were also present at the meeting.

During his visit, he is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and hold discussions on issues of mutual interest aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations.

item.title: PM orders completion of reopening, privatization of closed state-run factories by 2026
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday directed the authorities concerned to complete the process of reopening long-closed state-owned industrial units, accelerating their privatization and attracting private investment by 2026.
The directive came at a high-level meeting chaired by the prime minister at the Cabinet Division conference room in the Bangladesh Secretariat in the afternoon, according to the Prime Minister’s Press Wing.
The meeting reviewed measures to revive long-closed state-owned industrial establishments by removing bureaucratic hurdles, speeding up administrative processes and attracting domestic and foreign private investment to resume production.
The prime minister directed the authorities concerned to complete the process by the current calendar year.
The agencies concerned were also directed to take effective steps to create a more investment-friendly environment.
Prime Minister’s Finance and Planning Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, Commerce, Industries, and Textiles and Jute Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir, State Minister for Textiles and Jute Md Shariful Alam, Executive Chairman of the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) Ashik Chowdhury and senior officials from the relevant ministries and agencies were present.

item.title: Shama Obaed: No Bangladesh-Myanmar talks on repatriating 300,000 Rohingyas
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Thursday said there has been no discussion between the governments of Bangladesh and Myanmar regarding the reported repatriation of 300,000 Rohingyas from Bangladesh.
Her remarks came after Malaysian media reported that Myanmar had agreed to take back 300,000 Rohingya refugees from Bangladesh as part of ongoing repatriation efforts.
Speaking to reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Shama said Bangladesh would welcome such a development if it were confirmed.
"It will be very good news. I do not know anything specific yet," she said.
She added that Bangladesh remains in contact with Myanmar but no such issue has been discussed between the two governments.
The reports, quoting Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, said Myanmar had also agreed to repatriate 5,000 Rohingya refugees from Malaysia.
"That is why it is important to maintain good relations with Myanmar. They have now agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya from Malaysia and 300,000 Rohingya from Bangladesh to Myanmar," The Star quoted Anwar as saying.
"Why? Because we negotiated. These matters require careful diplomacy," he added while speaking at a meeting with local voters in Chennah on Wednesday.
Bangladesh currently hosts more than 1.3 million Rohingyas in camps in Cox's Bazar and on Bhasan Char after they fled persecution in Myanmar.

item.title: Dhipra death case: Withdrawal plea filed in court
item.description:
An application has been filed seeking to withdraw the case against four people, including the husband and in-laws of physician Nafisa Tabassum Dhipra, over her death in Dhaka's Dhanmondi.
The application was submitted on Wednesday to the court of Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Jewel Rana by the complainant, Mashiur Rahman Shah, who identified himself as Dhipra's relative.
Speaking on Thursday, complainant's lawyer Md Farhad Hossain Niyon said the complainant had applied to withdraw the case and that it was his personal decision.
"When an application for withdrawal is filed, it is usually heard on the scheduled date. The hearing in this case has been fixed for August 18," he said.
Asked about the reason behind the move, Mashiur Rahman told reporters: "No comments. Please wait. You will know on August 18."
On June 16, Mashiur filed the case accusing Dhipra's husband, Dr Rahmat Rashid, her father-in-law Dr Mohammad Abdur Rashid, head of the Cardiac Department at BIRDEM General Hospital, her mother-in-law Siddika Sultana, Shimu Naser, editor of the satire website Yarki, and several unnamed others.
The case alleged death by negligence, torture and concealment of evidence through burial without a post-mortem examination.
The court subsequently directed the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) to investigate the allegations.
According to the complaint, Dhipra married her classmate Dr Rahmat Rashid after a romantic relationship, and the couple has a two-year-old son.
It alleged that she had been subjected to physical and mental abuse by her husband's family since the marriage, causing her to suffer from severe depression. Following childbirth, she was also reportedly suffering from postpartum depression, high blood pressure and diabetes.
The complaint further alleged that despite being physicians, the accused failed to ensure her proper treatment and care and obstructed her preparation for the FCPS examination.
It also said that before her death, Dhipra had posted about domestic abuse in the Facebook group Female Doctors in Bangladesh.
The complaint claimed that Dhipra was locked inside a room for three consecutive days from June 2 without food and was prevented from seeing her two-year-old son.
On June 4, after being informed, her mother went to an apartment at Bashati Green Residence in Dhanmondi and found her daughter confined inside. After the door was opened, Dhipra embraced her mother and said: "Mother, I want to eat rice."
She then collapsed on the floor, the complaint said.
It further alleged that instead of taking her immediately to the nearest hospital, there was a delay in providing treatment, and she died on the way to BIRDEM General Hospital.
The case also alleged that after her death, efforts were made to suppress the incident by using influence to obtain a death certificate without conducting a post-mortem examination before arranging her burial.

item.title: Experts call for stronger role of nutritionists, dietitians in healthcare
item.description:
Health experts has underscored the need to strengthen the role of nutritionists and dietitians to improve public health, prevent non-communicable diseases and ensure evidence-based nutrition services across Bangladesh.
They said modernising clinical dietetic services and developing skilled human resources have become essential to improving patient care and accelerating recovery.
The observations came at a national dialogue titled ‘Advancement of Clinical Dietetics to Ensure Better Patient Care’ held at the CIRDAP auditorium in the capital on Wednesday.
The event was organised by Shushasther Bangladesh that brought together policymakers, physicians, nutritionists, dietitians, academics and researchers from the health, nutrition and education sectors.
Speaking as the chair, Dr Kazi Saifuddin Bennur, Chairman of Shushasther Bangladesh and Director of the Bangladesh Medical Research Council (BMRC), urged nutrition professionals to engage more actively in research.
He said the BMRC is ready to support them and stressed the need to translate research findings into entrepreneurship and public welfare initiatives.
Prime Minister’s Special Assistant on Health Affairs Dr S M Ziauddin Haider said both the quality and number of health professionals in the country must be increased.
“Our health system should not remain solely treatment-oriented. It must become prevention-focused,” he said, adding that nutritionists should play a stronger role in mainstream healthcare to ensure healthy longevity.
He also called for expanding the deployment of dietitians to the grassroots level, improving education standards, revising curricula and establishing a regulatory framework for the profession.
He said a dedicated regulatory system for dietitians would be introduced in the future.
The keynote paper was presented by Shamsunnahar Mahua, Chief Nutritionist at BIRDEM Hospital.
She said scientific nutrition services are playing an increasingly important role in preventing malnutrition, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease and cancer.
She stressed the need to develop skilled professionals, strengthen professional capacity and expand research in clinical nutrition.
The dialogue opened with welcome remarks from Syed Md Baki Billah Tutul, a member of Shushasther Bangladesh, and Tamanna Chowdhury, Principal Dietitian at Evercare Hospital.
The concluding remarks were delivered by Chowdhury Tasnim Hasin, Chief Dietitian at Continental Hospital.

item.title: Regent Group Chairman Shahed gets bail in Tk1cr fraud case
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Thursday granted bail to Regent Hospital and Regent Group Chairman Mohammad Shahed Karim in a fraud case filed over allegations of receiving construction materials worth Tk1 crore without making payment.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Mohammad Ehsanul Islam passed the order after a hearing on July 30.
Shahed’s lawyer Mohammad Dabir Uddin confirmed the matter, saying the court granted him a 10-day bail against a Tk5,000 bond on the condition of reaching a settlement with the complainant. However, he will not be released immediately as he is facing other cases. The case was filed on 13 July 2020 by Md Saifullah Masud, proprietor of Messrs Masud Enterprise.
According to the complaint, Shahed had been receiving construction materials from the firm since 2018. Although he initially made some cash payments, he later issued four cheques from Prime Bank worth a total of Tk1 crore for the supplies. The cheques were later dishonoured due to insufficient funds, the complaint said.
The complainant further alleged that Shahed repeatedly delayed payment despite being informed about the dishonoured cheques. On June 26, 2020, when the complainant went to demand payment, Shahed allegedly refused to pay and threatened him with death if he continued to press for the money. A general diary was later filed with Uttara West Police Station over the incident.
Meanwhile, Shahed was shown arrested in the case over the alleged fraud involving the unpaid Tk1 crore.
On July 20, Pallabi police arrested him from the ECB Chattar area in Dhaka in connection with a cheque dishonour case involving a Tk2.16 crore cheque issued by Mercantile Cooperative Bank.
Shahed has been in jail since his arrest. He faces more than 35 cases, including charges related to fraud, illegal arms possession and acquiring wealth beyond known sources of income. On 28 September 2020, he was sentenced to life imprisonment in an arms case. After securing bail in several cases, Shahed was released from prison on September4, 2024 after spending nearly four years behind bars.

item.title: GAU secures patent for jackfruit seed mineral concentrate technology
item.description:
Gazipur Agricultural University (GAU) has developed a patented technology to produce a mineral-rich food ingredient from jackfruit seeds, transforming an underutilised agricultural by-product into a value-added nutritional resource with potential applications in the food industry.
The innovation, jointly developed by Professor Dr Md Emdadul Haque of the Department of Food Engineering and postgraduate researcher Md Akram Hossain, has been granted a patent by the Department of Patents, Designs and Trademarks (DPDT) under the Ministry of Industries. The patent is registered as P/BD/2024/000040.
The invention, completed in November 2025 after three years of research under the guidance of GAU Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr GKM Mostafizur Rahman, is the university's first patented technology since it was renamed Gazipur Agricultural University. It also brings the institution's total number of patented technologies to 21.
The research was funded through the Ministry of Education's Grants for Advanced Research and Education (GARE) project.
According to the researchers, the technology increases the mineral concentration of dried jackfruit seeds from about 2% to more than 33%—a 16- to 17-fold increase—creating a concentrated ingredient suitable for use in fortified and processed foods.
Bangladesh is among the world's leading producers of jackfruit, yet large quantities of seeds and other by-products are discarded each year. The researchers said the technology offers a sustainable way to reduce food waste while creating new opportunities for value addition in the country's agro-processing sector.
The mineral concentrate contains essential nutrients, including potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, iron, zinc and manganese, which are vital for bone health, blood formation, immune function, and normal muscle and nerve function.
"The mineral concentrate can be incorporated into processed foods to enhance their nutritional value while reducing agricultural waste and supporting food and nutrition security," said Professor Dr Emdadul Haque.
He added that commercialising the technology could accelerate the development of nutrient-enriched food products, expand jackfruit-based industries, increase farmers' incomes and promote more efficient utilisation of agricultural resources.
GAU Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr GKM Mostafizur Rahman described the patent as "a milestone for Bangladesh's agricultural, food and nutrition research," saying it demonstrates how agricultural waste can be transformed into a high-value nutritional resource.

item.title: Heavy rains ravage Faridpur chilli fields, prices soar
item.description:
Prolonged heavy rainfall has devastated summer chilli cultivation in Faridpur's Madhukhali upazila, destroying large swathes of farmland, leaving thousands of growers counting heavy losses, and pushing retail prices of the spice to as high as Tk320 per kilogram.
Once carpeted with lush green chilli plants, fields across the upazila now lie waterlogged after more than a week of incessant rain, with rotting plants and failed crops replacing what had promised to be a productive season.
Madhukhali Upazila Agriculture Officer Md Mahbub Elahi said summer chilli was cultivated on around 2,720 hectares this season, but excessive rainfall submerged most fields, causing widespread crop damage.
"Waterlogging has caused chilli plants to rot and die in most of the cultivated areas. We are preparing a list of affected farmers. Some have already received government assistance, while others will be brought under compensation programmes in phases," he said.
According to local farmers, nearly three-quarters of the chilli fields have been damaged, with Raipur, Jahapur and Meghchami unions suffering the worst losses.
Farmers, including Rokonuzzaman and Firoz Mia of Raipur Union, said they had no option but to uproot their crops after the plants died.
"Almost all our chilli plants have perished due to the heavy rain. We have been forced to clear the fields," they said.
They said cultivation costs had already risen sharply because of higher prices of seeds, fertilisers and pesticides. With the crop wiped out, many farmers are unlikely to recover even half of their investment.
"If the government provides financial support, we will be able to resume cultivation," they added.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), chilli has been cultivated on 3,112 hectares across Faridpur district this season, with a production target of 5,706 tonnes. Officials now fear the target will not be met because of the widespread damage caused by continuous rainfall.
The production shortfall has also driven up prices in local markets.
A visit to Haji Shariatullah Market, Chakbazar, Tepakhola Market and Helipad Market in Faridpur town found green chilli retailing at Tk280-Tk320 per kg, depending on quality.
Retail traders said supplies had fallen sharply as rain-damaged fields yielded little produce, resulting in steep price increases.
Faridpur Krishak Samity President Advocate Manik Majumdar urged the government to provide immediate compensation and rehabilitation support to affected farmers.
"There is hardly any chilli left in the fields, yet prices continue to climb. If affected farmers are not supported quickly, many may be discouraged from cultivating chilli next season," he said.

item.title: In the Caspian Sea, the Ukraine and Iran wars collide
item.description:
A large inland sea connecting military supply lines through Russia and Iran could now be a pivotal theatre for two major wars that are usually thought of as separate.
Over the weekend, Kyiv’s main domestic intelligence agency, the SBU, said Ukrainian drones hit a Russian missile boat as well as two cargo ships in the Caspian Sea that “were under international sanctions and were used to transport military cargo between Iran and Russia.”
Iranian officials immediately disputed the assertion, saying Ukraine hit a commercial vessel carrying iron and killed one sailor.
As the two sides fought over the origins of the targeted vessels, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei vowed revenge and summoned Ukraine’s top diplomat in Tehran in protest, in what appeared to be a sign of the two wars colliding in a new front.
For more than five months, global attention has been focused on another Middle Eastern waterway, the Strait of Hormuz, as the Iranian regime threatened freedom of navigation of commercial ships and placed pressure on the world’s energy markets.
But analysts say the latest attacks in the Caspian Sea indicate the Ukraine war and the Iran war are not isolated theatres, but parts of an “emerging Eurasian conflict system in which Russia and Iran are mutually dependent.”
And it is through a 371,000-square-kilometre area that those two conflicts intersect, Basil Germond, professor of international security at Lancaster University, told the ABC.
The Caspian Sea is the largest landlocked body of water in the world and is bordered by Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Iran.
Because of its geographical position, it is often out of reach and off the radar of most of the world, but historically it has been an important East–West trading route, dating back to Imperial China and the Silk Road.
Russia has long used it as a platform for “long-range power projection” and as a sanction-immune bridge to its ally, Iran.
“This sea is not a sea where Western powers can really exercise any form of leverage,”
Professor Germond said.
Since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Caspian Sea has become even more important as a “safe haven” for Russia’s Black Sea-based naval forces to relocate after major attacks.
A river and lock network connects the two seas, allowing warships “of a certain size” to travel between them, Professor Germond said.
“Some of the Russian assets have been relocated to the Caspian and it was considered as safe,” he added.
But Ukraine’s intervention over the weekend has likely shattered the assumption of safety in the inland sea.
Analysts say Kyiv’s ability to project more than 692 kilometers from Ukraine’s nearest border into Russia and Iran’s “safe space” indicates the two conflicts remain in danger of colliding and escalating.
And with the Caspian Sea now in play, what happens in this theatre next could have ramifications for not just one war, but two.
Tensions between Iran and Ukraine have existed for some time and largely center around Tehran’s support for Russia’s military campaign.
Since 2022, Iran has supplied lethal long-range attack drones that Moscow has used to degrade Ukraine’s air defenses and target its power and water infrastructure.
The supply of these crucial weapons, called Shaheds, has been facilitated via the Caspian Sea through Russian and Iranian ports.
“The import of drones or drone components from Iran [through the inland sea] up until quite recently was considered as a safe route,” Professor Germond said.
“But that has changed now.”
Russia has since developed its own version of the drones with special enhancements, and begun manufacturing them in-country, making it less reliant on Iranian drone shipments.
But the collaboration between the two nations is not limited to one side. In exchange for Iran’s equipment, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Russia of providing Tehran with satellite surveillance of Gulf states and US military bases in the region to help it coordinate attacks.
“It’s clear that the two countries are collaborating militarily,” Professor Germond said.
“Being able to rely on its allies [Iran] is instrumental in enabling [Russia] to continue their war and also to sustain their war economy.
By targeting the Caspian, however, Kyiv is attempting to disrupt that partnership and distract its enemies by forcing them to divert their much-needed war supplies to other areas.
“If Ukraine is targeting Russian or Iranian assets in the Caspian, then the Russians, and the Iranians for that matter, have to reallocate air defense systems in the Caspian. So then they can’t use that elsewhere,” Professor Germond said.
Yet after the attacks, Mr Zelensky said Ukraine should avoid actions that could open an additional front in the space.
“We must be careful. We must do everything to ensure that under no circumstances do we open a new front, but we must be honest. The Iranians and the North Koreans have already attacked us,” he told Sky News.
He warned Ukraine would be prepared for any development from Iran.
The Caspian Sea might be in the global spotlight because of Ukraine’s recent strikes, but it has been targeted before.
Last August, Ukraine conducted a long-range drone attack on a supply ship in the Caspian port of Olya, which it claimed was loaded with drone components and Iranian munitions.
And in March, Israel targeted dozens of Iranian assets along the Caspian coastline, including missile boats, a shipyard ‌used ⁠to build and repair vessels, and a command center.
“What Ukraine is trying to do is to show that they can exercise … [a] type of leverage there, because if vessels in the Caspian think it’s too dangerous, if there are many attacks, then the two countries, Russia and Iran, will have to rely on a terrestrial route that’s less good for many reasons,” Professor Germond said.
If the tactic sounds familiar, it is because Tehran has used a similar strategy with great effect in the Strait of Hormuz.
Ukraine’s strikes fell on the eve of Mr Zelensky’s visit to the United States, and Professor Germond said the timing of the two events is significant and may have been designed to generate support for Kyiv within the Trump administration.
Ahead of his visit, Mr Zelensky had warned of Russia and Iran’s close military collaboration and told Sky News that Tehran had been responsible for transferring new technologies to Moscow.
“I think in the current context, it’s quite obvious that it’s a way to demonstrate to Trump that the winner is Zelensky, not Vladimir Putin,” Professor Germond said.
“Zelensky is currently managing to convince Trump that he’s the strong man, and that’s important because Ukraine still depends on weapons and support from the West in general, the US in particular,” Professor Germond said.
The Ukrainian leader met with Mr Trump on Tuesday, local time, and said the two leaders discussed securing more air defense capabilities for Kyiv and “several other ideas that could help.”
For some time now, technologies and materials relevant to sustaining both Iran and Russia’s war economies have moved through the Caspian Sea.
That is partly because it is insulated from Western sanction pressure, with a treaty of cooperation struck between the five countries that border the Caspian stipulating that no nation can grant entry to third-party military assets.
“It means that none of those countries around the Caspian Sea is allowed to ask, for example, the US to send military assets to the Caspian. It wouldn’t be legal,”
Professor Germond said.
The Caspian Sea therefore functions as a critical node for Russia and Iran.
“For Russia, because of the sanctions since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the Caspian Sea has become more important for trade. And for Iran, it’s the same,” Professor Germond said.
For its part, Iran has condemned Ukraine’s attack.
In a post on X, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called the strikes on ships “a blatant UN Charter violation” and claimed it had been “done at Israel’s behest to drag Europe into its war.” He offered no evidence to support the allegation.
Mr Araghchi said he had also discussed the incident with both the European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
He said he made clear that Ukraine’s action “cannot go unanswered.”

Study: Post-Covid job hunt gets difficult as competition rises by 66%
item.description:
Competition in the country's job market is now significantly higher than at any point in the past.
Currently, an average of 287 job seekers are applying for a single position posted on online job portals.
In contrast, during the five years preceding the Covid-19 pandemic, there were an average of 173 applicants per position.
This means that job competition has increased by nearly 66% in the post-pandemic era.
These findings were revealed in a study jointly conducted by the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) and the General Economics Division (GED) of the Planning Commission.
The results of the research were presented on Thursday during a seminar titled "Labor Market in Tough Times and Macroeconomic Shocks: Evidence from the Largest Online Job Portal," organized by BIDS in the capital.
Chaired by BIDS Director General AK Enamul Haque, the seminar was attended by State Minister for Planning Md Zonaed Abdur Rahim Saki as the chief guest.
BIDS research director Atanu Rabbani presented the research paper. He stated that the study analyzed 10 years and 6 months of data (from 2015 to 2025) from the country's largest online job portal.
According to the study, the country's labor market faced its biggest shock during the lockdown period of the Covid-19 pandemic.
At that time, job circulars dropped by nearly 70%, and job applications fell by 59%. It took nearly nine and a half months for the labor market to fully normalize.
However, even after the impact of the pandemic subsided, competition in the job market increased significantly and has now reached a record level.
Atanu Rabbani noted that currently, 85%-89% of total employment in the country remains in the informal sector.
A small fraction of formal sector jobs—around 2.5% to 3%—are recruited through online job portals. Although this segment is relatively small, online job data provides swift signals regarding shifts in the labor market, which can play a vital role in policy-making.
He shared that over the last 10 years, an average of 1,154 job circulars were published per week, offering opportunities across an average of 3,646 positions.
In response, an average of approximately 697,000 job seekers applied each week.
While most recruitments were for entry-level positions, there was a higher tendency toward direct hiring for upper-level roles.
Additionally, 54% of the job postings did not specify any gender requirements.
Atanu Rabbani added that monetary policy over the past decade has failed to generate a significant positive impact on the labour market. Expanding credit facilities alone cannot drive employment growth. The pace of new investments and job creation remains limited.
As a result, hiring for existing positions is low, unemployment pressure is rising, and applicants are having to wait much longer than before to land a job.
State Minister for Planning Md Zonaed Abdur Rahim Saki stated that alongside recovering a fragile economy, the government is implementing various skill development programs to build a skilled workforce.
He noted that to build a production-oriented and investment-driven economy, the government has taken steps to diversify investment sectors, with plans to expand employment by increasing investments in at least 10 new sectors.
BIDS director general AK Enamul Haque stated that various global crises, including the Covid-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, have deeply impacted Bangladesh's labour market. The employment situation deteriorated further in July–August 2024. Although there was a slight improvement in the second half of 2025, the country's labor market continues to navigate harsh realities due to lingering post-Covid economic pressures.

item.description:

“Recent news reports claiming that 5,000 Bangladeshis have had their visas cancelled in the UAE are inaccurate. According to official data, exactly 626 Bangladeshis have experienced "auto-cancellation" of their visas so far,” she told reporters at a joint briefing with State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Md Nurul Haque at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Earlier, they had an inter-ministerial meeting at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Shama Obaed said the situation is not specific to Bangladesh and citizens of other countries, including Nepal, Pakistan, Egypt, and the Philippines, have also faced visa cancellations for various reasons.
“Out of the 626 affected Bangladeshis, details of 417 individuals have already been submitted to the UAE government for visa renewals. Information for the remaining individuals is being processed and forwarded systematically,” she said.
If visas were cancelled due to job termination, the respective employers bear certain responsibilities, said the state minister.
The Bangladeshi Embassy in the UAE is directly coordinating with these companies to find viable solutions, she added.
“We hope we will get a positive result,” said the state minister, encouraging the media to report based on verified facts.
Shama Obaed said expatriates must strictly respect and follow the laws of their host country and refrain from engaging in unlawful activities or posting sensitive or political content on social media platforms. “We want to send out a message - please refrain from engaging in unlawful activities.”
Many migrant workers go abroad after making immense financial sacrifices, and when individuals submit fraudulent or forged documents, it harms the country's reputation and creates hurdles for those attempting to travel legally, she said.
Shama Obaed said the government will consider amendments, if required, to the relevant law to enforce stricter measures against document forgery.
Migration costs from Bangladesh remain significantly higher than those from neighbouring countries like Nepal.
The government has initiated active measures to reduce migration expenses and protect workers from fraudulent middlemen networks.
For the first time in history, Shama Obaed said, a dedicated "Migration and NRB Affairs Wing" has been established within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to curb illegal migration and human trafficking.

item.description:
Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has allocated Tk50.5 crore for mosquito control insecticides in its Tk4,004.6 crore budget for FY2026-27 after a pre-monsoon survey found Aedes mosquito larval density above the prescribed index in 63 of its 75 wards.
The survey identified 27 wards as high-risk areas, where the corporation carried out special crash programs ahead of the monsoon, according to DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam.
Salam unveiled the budget at the DSCC Nagar Bhaban auditorium on Thursday.
The allocation for mosquito control insecticides has increased from Tk45.35 crore in the original FY2025-26 budget. However, the amount was later revised down to Tk30.35 crore.
The FY2026-27 budget also earmarks Tk4 crore for diesel, petrol, oil and lubricants to support mosquito control operations, a category that had no separate allocation in the previous fiscal year's budget.
Another Tk2 crore has been allocated for transportation expenses, including the movement of fogger and wheel spray machines, up from Tk1.5 crore in FY2025-26.
In addition, Tk7.5 crore has been set aside for mosquito control machinery and equipment, compared with Tk2 crore in the revised budget for the previous fiscal year.
In his budget speech, Salam said DSCC had stepped up mosquito control and dengue prevention efforts through regular larviciding in the morning and adulticiding in the afternoon across all wards.
He said mosquito workers and supervisors had received training, while a cross-departmental monitoring team had been formed to ensure mosquito control activities were carried out according to standard procedures.
Salam also said tests conducted by the Ministry of Health found the insecticides currently used by the corporation to be 100% effective. Recommendations from expert teams on alternative insecticides and mosquito control methods were also being implemented regularly, he added.
The administrator said DSCC continued to conduct awareness campaigns through schools and colleges, social media, television commercials, religious institutions and newspaper notices, alongside region-based cleanliness drives involving local public representatives.
"We believe public participation is the greatest tool in preventing dengue," he said.
The Tk4,004.6 crore budget for FY2026-27 was approved at the 14th meeting of the DSCC Governing Committee on July 26.
For FY2025-26, DSCC had originally approved a Tk3,841.38 crore budget, which was later revised to Tk3,138.77 crore.

item.title: Rose Garden: A historic treasure in the heart of Old Dhaka
item.description:
Tucked away amid the bustling streets of Old Dhaka, the historic Rose Garden Palace stands as an enduring symbol of the city's architectural grandeur, aristocratic legacy and political history.
More than a century after its construction, the stately mansion continues to captivate visitors with its elegant design while preserving the stories of a bygone era.
Located on KM Das Lane in Tikatuli, the Rose Garden was once a prestigious residence of Dhaka's elite. Surrounded by lush gardens, ornamental ponds, fountains and intricate decorative elements, the palace remains one of the capital's finest examples of heritage architecture.
A Legacy born in the late 19th century
The Rose Garden traces its origins to the late 19th century, when zamindar(Feudal landlord) Hrishikesh Das commissioned the construction of the palatial residence along with an adjoining rose garden. By the 1930s, the estate had earned widespread recognition for its collection of rose varieties imported from different parts of the world, giving rise to the name "Rose Garden."
Spread across nearly seven acres, the estate was designed to reflect the grandeur of the era. Its imposing central dome, towering Corinthian-style columns, ornate windows, crystal chandeliers and landscaped gardens have made it one of Dhaka's most distinguished historic landmarks.
An architectural masterpiece
The palace showcases a harmonious blend of European architectural influences and local craftsmanship. A spacious forecourt, ornamental pond, sculptures and decorative motifs create an impressive entrance, while stained-glass windows, intricately carved columns and sparkling crystal chandeliers add to its timeless elegance.
In its heyday, the Rose Garden served as a vibrant social and cultural venue, hosting lavish receptions, musical soirées and gatherings of the city's aristocracy.
Preserving a national treasure
Despite changes in ownership over the decades, the Rose Garden has retained its historical and cultural significance.
Recognising its exceptional heritage value, the Department of Archaeology declared the palace a protected monument in 1989. The Government of Bangladesh later acquired the property in 2018, reaffirming its commitment to preserving one of the country's most treasured historic landmarks.
An enduring attraction for visitors
Today, the Rose Garden Palace remains one of Old Dhaka's most cherished heritage attractions. Drawing history enthusiasts, architecture lovers and travellers alike, it offers visitors a rare glimpse into the elegance of the zamindari era and the rich cultural legacy of the old city.
With its seamless blend of history, architecture and political significance, the Rose Garden Palace continues to stand as a living monument to Dhaka's glorious past, preserving memories of a bygone age while inspiring future generations to appreciate and protect the nation's heritage.

item.title: Rizvi stresses rule of law to combat human trafficking
item.description:
BNP Senior Joint Secretary General and Political Adviser to the Prime Minister Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Thursday underscored the need for stronger anti-human trafficking laws and the effective enforcement of the rule of law, saying trafficking networks flourish where justice is weak.
Addressing a discussion at the RC Majumdar Auditorium of the Theatre Building at the University of Dhaka, Rizvi said human trafficking syndicates are deeply rooted in society and can only be dismantled through impartial law enforcement.
"The government's priority should be to eliminate human trafficking networks, irrespective of their influence or connections," he said.
Emphasising that security is a fundamental right of every citizen, Rizvi warned that poor and lower-middle-income people would continue to fall prey to exploitation and modern-day slavery unless the state ensured legal protection and justice.
He said the lack of the rule of law has fuelled injustice and oppression at the grassroots, where many semi-literate and illiterate people are unable to access local authorities or assert their rights, leaving them particularly vulnerable to exploitation.
He said the state must fulfil its responsibility to protect society, observing that people from developing and Third World countries are among the most frequent victims of human trafficking.
Stressing the need for stronger action, Rizvi said the government must enact tougher anti-human trafficking laws and ensure the effective enforcement of the rule of law to curb the crime.
Rizvi said many people, unaware of the risks, sell their land to brokers and fraudulent agents in the hope of securing jobs abroad, only to become victims of human trafficking.
"After losing everything to trafficking syndicates, many are deported because of legal complications during transit or after reaching their destination. They return home with neither assets nor any means of livelihood," he said.
He said human trafficking is driven by a combination of political and social factors, identifying statelessness, limited economic opportunities and displacement as among its principal causes.
Linking child marriage and inadequate education to the crime, Rizvi said those forced into early marriage often become parents at a young age and are unable to continue their education.
"Without education, they are deprived of opportunities to become self-reliant and improve their lives, making them far more vulnerable to human trafficking," he added.

item.title: Rajuk faces scrutiny over new sewage rules
item.description:
The government’s latest directive requiring buildings in Gulshan, Banani, Baridhara, and Niketan to install septic tanks, soak wells, and, in some cases, sewage treatment plants (STPs) has sparked debate over whether authorities are tackling environmental pollution or shifting the cost of years of planning and regulatory shortcomings onto property owners.
While Rajuk says the move is essential to stop untreated wastewater from polluting Gulshan Lake and groundwater, urban planners argue the directive has exposed deeper weaknesses in Dhaka’s building regulation, sewerage planning, and enforcement systems.
Under Bangladesh’s planning framework, Rajuk is responsible for approving building designs, ensuring compliance with construction rules, and verifying buildings before occupancy.
Experts question how thousands of buildings were approved if the wastewater management systems now being required were already mandatory under existing regulations.
“If mandatory sanitation facilities were absent, how were occupancy certificates issued in the first place?” asked one urban planning expert, arguing that regulatory failures cannot now be shifted entirely onto citizens.
Many property owners say they constructed their buildings according to Rajuk-approved designs, obtained legal utility connections, and have paid sewerage charges to Dhaka WASA for years.
They are now being instructed to retrofit expensive sanitation systems that may require significant structural modifications.
“We fully support protecting Gulshan Lake,” said a property owner in Gulshan, requesting anonymity.
“But if the authorities approved these buildings, connected them to the sewerage system, and collected sewerage fees for years, why are we now being told our sanitation systems are inadequate?”
The controversy has also revived questions about Bangladesh’s unfinished sewerage infrastructure.
The Tk3,482-crore Dasherkandi Sewage Treatment Plant, inaugurated in 2023, was expected to form the backbone of Dhaka’s modern wastewater management system. However, much of the capital remains outside the central sewerage network, leaving many neighborhoods dependent on decentralized wastewater disposal.
Urban planners question whether requiring costly building-level STPs before completing the city’s sewerage network reflects a coherent long-term strategy.
“Decentralized mandates without completing central sewerage reflect fragmented urban governance and shift responsibility to citizens,” said Adil Mohammed Khan, executive director of the Institute for Planning and Development (IPD) and a professor in the Department of Urban and Regional Planning at Jahangirnagar University.
Architect and urban development expert Iqbal Habib echoed those concerns, saying Dhaka’s sanitation crisis cannot be solved “building by building” but instead requires integrated citywide infrastructure planning backed by institutional accountability.
Urban governance specialists say sewerage systems, like roads and drainage, are core public infrastructure.
They argue that if the state has yet to complete the necessary network, requiring individual property owners to bear the full financial burden raises important policy questions.
Several experts recommend phased implementation, government incentives, technical assistance, and cost-sharing mechanisms rather than blanket compliance orders.
Rajuk, however, maintains that immediate intervention is necessary.
Chief Town Planner Mohammad Ashraful Islam said the 2025 Building Construction Rules require STPs in areas lacking effective sewerage coverage, while septic tanks and soak wells remain mandatory under the rules, even in areas served by sewer lines.
According to Rajuk, Dhaka’s existing sewerage coverage remains insufficient to rely solely on centralized treatment, making decentralized systems essential until the network is fully developed.
Environmental experts caution that residential buildings are only one of several sources of pollution entering Gulshan Lake.
Wastewater from commercial establishments, informal settlements, illegal sewer connections, stormwater drains, and aging infrastructure also contributes significantly to deteriorating water quality.
Previous surveys have identified numerous drainage outlets discharging untreated wastewater into the lake, suggesting the pollution originates from multiple sources rather than households alone.
Experts therefore call for comprehensive pollution mapping, independent technical audits of existing buildings, faster expansion of the central sewerage network, accelerated connections to the Dasherkandi treatment plant, and transparent enforcement based on scientific evidence.
Beyond septic tanks and STPs, they say the controversy raises broader questions about urban governance, regulatory accountability, and the state’s responsibility to provide essential public infrastructure.
While protecting Gulshan Lake is widely recognized as an environmental necessity, experts say long-term restoration will require more than stricter compliance.
It will also depend on coordinated investment, institutional accountability, and a clear, evidence-based strategy for expanding Dhaka’s sewerage infrastructure.

item.title: Why Fiji’s HIV surge matters for Bangladesh
item.description:
Thousands of Bangladeshi workers in Fiji and the country’s rapidly expanding HIV epidemic have prompted global health experts to urge Bangladesh and other Asian nations to strengthen harm reduction and HIV prevention before similar outbreaks take hold.
Speaking at the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026), experts pointed to Fiji’s experience as a warning of how quickly HIV can spread when infections among people who inject drugs are not brought under control.
The Pacific island nation, which now employs between 3,000 and 3,500 Bangladeshi workers, has recorded a 14-fold increase in new HIV diagnoses over the past five years.
The outbreak became so severe that Fiji declared a national HIV outbreak in January 2025 after infections spread from people who inject drugs into the wider population.
Responding to a question from Dhaka Tribune, Dr Jason Mitchell, chair of Fiji’s National HIV Outbreak Cluster Response Taskforce, said health authorities are monitoring HIV infections among migrant workers, although nationality-specific data are not available.
Experts said Fiji’s experience carries an important lesson for Bangladesh, where HIV prevalence remains low but continued investment in harm reduction is essential to prevent future outbreaks.
Md Akhtaruzzaman, senior manager for Management and Coordination at the AIDS/STD Program under the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), said Bangladesh’s situation differs significantly because most yaba and methamphetamine users consume the drugs orally rather than by injection.
He said Bangladesh has an estimated 34,000 people who inject drugs, about 87% of whom are covered by harm reduction services, including needle and syringe exchange programs and methadone maintenance treatment.
“Our HIV program places strong emphasis on people who inject drugs through targeted harm reduction interventions,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
“Sustaining these services is essential for preventing HIV, sexually transmitted infections and hepatitis C.”
According to UNAIDS data presented at the conference, Fiji’s adult HIV prevalence has reached 1.2%, while the number of people living with HIV has risen from about 8,900 in 2025 to an estimated 12,000 this year.
Nearly two-thirds of new infections are among people aged 20 to 34.
The country’s treatment response has also fallen well short of global targets, with only about 40% of people living with HIV aware of their status, 22% receiving treatment and just 3.2% achieving viral suppression.
Dr Mitchell said the absence of a nationwide needle and syringe program remains one of the biggest gaps in Fiji’s response, allowing HIV transmission among people who inject drugs to continue.
Experts at AIDS 2026 said Fiji’s outbreak illustrates how rapidly HIV can spread beyond key populations if prevention, testing and treatment fail to keep pace with changing patterns of drug use.
They warned that maintaining evidence-based harm reduction programs is far less costly than responding to a rapidly expanding epidemic after it has spread into the general population.

item.title: Inside Salahuddin Ammar’s rise at Rajshahi University
item.description:
From forcing deans to resign and confronting university authorities to repeated allegations of violence, intimidation and administrative interference, Rucsu General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar has remained at the centre of one controversy after another.
A fresh attempted murder case has now raised broader questions over whether repeated institutional inaction emboldened one of the country’s most controversial student leaders.
For nearly a year, Rajshahi University has witnessed a steady stream of controversies surrounding Rajshahi University Central Students’ Union (Rucsu) General Secretary Salahuddin Ammar.
Each incident sparked criticism, protests or investigation committees. Yet none resulted in visible disciplinary action.
That pattern has now come under renewed scrutiny after a court directed the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) to investigate an attempted murder case against Ammar, Rucsu Assistant General Secretary SM Salman Sabbir and seven other student leaders over the alleged assault on student Mahmudul Hasan inside the university’s central library.
The case also names 17 to 18 unidentified people as accused.
The criminal case is the most serious legal challenge Ammar has faced since emerging as one of the most influential student leaders on campus.
But for many teachers and students, it is only the latest chapter in a series of incidents that they say gradually transformed him from an elected student representative into a figure capable of influencing administrative decisions and creating a climate of fear across the university.
According to the case filed by Mahmudul’s father, the victim was repeatedly assaulted with iron rods and bamboo sticks, dragged from an ambulance while being taken for treatment and beaten again.
The complaint further alleges that when the family first approached Motihar Police Station, police declined to accept the case, prompting them to seek relief through the court, which later referred the matter to the PBI for investigation.
Long before the latest case, Ammar had repeatedly drawn headlines.
During protests over the reinstatement of the “dependent quota” before the Rucsu election, he led demonstrations in which the then vice-chancellor’s vehicle was surrounded and university officials were confined inside an administrative building for hours.
The incident triggered widespread criticism, although Ammar denied physically assaulting any teacher.
After becoming Rucsu general secretary, allegations against him shifted from street protests to university administration.
Teachers accused him of interfering in administrative affairs, threatening faculty members and publicly pressuring deans to resign.
During one protest, resignation letters were displayed before journalists while administrative offices, including those of the vice-chancellor, registrar and proctor, were locked.
The university later relieved several deans of their duties following the standoff.
His activities also extended beyond campus administration.
A fundraising campaign seeking Tk76 lakh for a July anniversary concert drew criticism over transparency.
An eight-hour railway blockade over an unrelated student incident disrupted train services across the western region and, according to railway authorities, caused losses of around Tk35 lakh.
Controversial social media comments and political disputes further fuelled public debate.
Critics also repeatedly linked Ammar to earlier incidents of violence, including allegations over the death of a former Chhatra League leader in 2024.
Those allegations have been publicly denied by Ammar, and no conviction has been reported.
Despite the succession of controversies, university authorities acknowledge that while several investigation committees were formed over different incidents, their findings never resulted in publicly known disciplinary measures.
Teachers and student organisations argue that this lack of visible accountability allowed tensions to escalate over time.
The latest library assault has intensified those concerns.
The Democratic Student Alliance described the incident as “mob violence” and demanded a fair investigation.
Leaders of the Student Rights Council, Samajtantrik Chhatra Front and Chhatra Dal also called for those responsible to be punished, warning that repeated incidents were undermining the university’s academic environment and damaging its reputation nationwide.
Ammar has rejected the allegations, saying all of his actions were intended to protect students’ interests.
He claimed the library violence was a reaction to an attack on the Rucsu building by Chhatra League activists.
Rajshahi University Chhatra Shibir also denied responsibility for his actions, saying he is not a member of the organisation.
University authorities say the latest incident, along with earlier allegations, is now under investigation and that action will be taken once inquiry reports are submitted.
For many on campus, however, the central question is no longer about a single incident, but how repeated controversies were allowed to accumulate until they culminated in a criminal investigation.
