item.title: DU suspends 3 teachers, relieves four others of key duties
item.description:
Three teachers of the University of Dhaka have been temporarily suspended, while four others have been relieved of all academic and administrative responsibilities over separate allegations of misconduct and irregularities.
The university’s Public Relations Office confirmed the decisions in a statement issued on Thursday, following a syndicate meeting held on July 28.
The meeting was chaired by Dhaka University Vice-Chancellor Professor Dr ABM Obaidul Islam.
The suspended teachers are Professor Dr Sadeka Halim of the Department of Sociology, Professor Dr Md Shafiqul Islam of the Department of Nuclear Engineering, and Professor Dr Afroza Shelly.
Professor Sadeka Halim was suspended over allegations of unprofessional conduct inside and outside the classroom, ethical misconduct and other related issues. The other two teachers were suspended based on complaints from students of different batches and based on the findings of an inquiry committee.
The syndicate also removed Professor Dr Md Abdul Muhit of the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology from the post of department chairman and barred him from all academic and administrative duties over allegations of activities against the spirit of the July mass uprising, spreading propaganda against the university administration and the government, supporting a banned organisation, and issuing threats.
Prof Dr Abu Shara Shamsur Rouf of the Department of Pharmaceutical Technology and Prof Dr Rafiqul Islam (Rafiq Shahariar) of the Department of Peace and Conflict Studies were also relieved of all academic and administrative responsibilities over similar allegations.
Professor Dr Mohammad Bahauddin of the Department of Persian Language and Literature was relieved of his duties over allegations of departmental irregularities and plagiarism in MPhil and PhD theses.
The syndicate formed a committee, led by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Education) Professor Dr Abdus Salam, to review alleged irregularities in the university’s recruitment process between January 2009 and June 2024 and assess the transparency of appointments. The deans of all faculties have been included in the committee.
Another committee, headed by Pro-VC (Administration) Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane, was formed to review research activities conducted under the Higher Education Quality Enhancement Project (HEQEP), funded by the World Bank and the University Grants Commission, during the same period and examine whether project funds were properly utilised.
The Syndicate also decided to take action against individuals, groups and organisations allegedly involved in activities contrary to the spirit of the July mass uprising. It said further decisions will be taken after verification.
In a separate decision, the Syndicate suspended AKM Mahbub Mustafa, supervising engineer (Civil) at the Office of the Chief Engineer, over allegations of activities violating office discipline.
The meeting approved the construction of a July Memorial at the Mall Chattar adjacent to the university's administrative building in memory of those killed during the July mass uprising. The foundation stone of the monument is scheduled to be unveiled on August 5.

item.title: Spider-Man’s loneliest chapter yet
item.description:
This year has been a milestone for Tom Holland.
From getting engaged to longtime partner Zendaya to returning to the role that made him a global star, the British actor seems to be living a life that once existed only in his dreams.
The boy who famously wished to become Spider-Man eventually got to wear the suit.
Now, nearly a decade after his Marvel debut, he is swinging back for another chapter.
Peter Parker, however, has had no such happy ending.
At the close of Spider-Man: No Way Home, the teenager who once had friends, family and mentors was erased from everyone’s memory.
MJ no longer knows him.
Ned Leeds has forgotten their friendship.
Even Doctor Strange’s spell has wiped Peter Parker from the world’s consciousness.
The beloved superhero is left with nothing but his identity as Spider-Man.
That heartbreaking ending sets the stage for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, arriving four years after the events of No Way Home.
The title suggests hope, but for Peter, a “brand new day” means rebuilding his life from absolute zero.
If the film’s trailers and officially revealed details are any indication, that fresh start will be anything but peaceful.
Frank Castle, better known as the Punisher, joins the story as a morally complex ally whose uncompromising brand of justice is likely to clash with Spider-Man’s ideals.
Jon Bernthal reprises the role after his acclaimed appearances in Marvel’s Daredevil series, bringing one of the franchise’s most uncompromising antiheroes into Peter Parker’s world.
The film also welcomes the return of Tombstone, one of New York’s most powerful crime bosses, while Scorpion finally resurfaces after his brief appearance in Spider-Man: Homecoming, promising to settle unfinished business with the web-slinger.
Perhaps the biggest mystery, however, surrounds Bruce Banner.
Promotional footage has teased an enraged Hulk confronting Spider-Man and the Punisher, raising questions about what could push Banner back into losing control.
Meanwhile, Sadie Sink joins the cast in a role Marvel has kept tightly under wraps, fuelling widespread speculation among fans.
Beyond its expanding roster of heroes and villains, Brand New Day reunites the cast that helped define the previous trilogy.
Tom Holland returns as Peter Parker alongside Zendaya as MJ and Jacob Batalon as Ned Leeds.
Their reunion carries particular emotional weight after No Way Home ended with Peter choosing not to reveal himself to the two people who mattered most to him.
The supporting cast also brings together some of the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s most recognisable faces, including Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner and Jon Bernthal as Frank Castle.
As a result, Brand New Day feels less like a conventional Spider-Man sequel and more like a crossover that could reshape Peter Parker’s place within the wider MCU.
For many viewers, the film also marks the return of a Spider-Man they have grown up with.
Audiences who first met Holland’s Peter Parker in Captain America: Civil War in 2016 have watched the character evolve from an eager teenager desperate to impress Iron Man into a hero defined by sacrifice and loss.
Along the way, Peter has lost his mentor Tony Stark, his Aunt May, his closest friends and, ultimately, his place in the world.
That emotional journey may prove to be Brand New Day’s greatest strength.
For the first time in Holland’s Spider-Man saga, Peter has no safety net. No mentor. No Avengers to rely on. No friends waiting at the end of the battle.
He has to discover who Spider-Man is when no one remembers Peter Parker.
Filmed across New York City, Glasgow and Basingstoke, the movie also returns the character to the city that has always been central to his identity.
Yet its biggest question is not where Peter will go next or which villain he will face.
It is who he will become.
Tom Holland once dreamed of becoming Spider-Man.
Now he returns to portray a Peter Parker who has lost almost everything except the mask.
Perhaps that is what Brand New Day truly means.
After losing everything that once defined him, Peter must decide what kind of hero remains when there is no one left to remember the boy behind the mask.

item.title: Experts: Institutionalizing early disability identification can transform lives
item.description:
Early identification and intervention for children with disabilities should be institutionalized to improve lifelong outcomes and reduce social and economic costs, experts said at a June 24 roundtable organized by the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD) with Liliane Fonds.
Findings from a 2024–2026 project in Barguna and Chattogram showed early screening boosted access to healthcare, rehabilitation, education and social protection, while strengthening caregiver confidence. But limited specialist services, weak referrals, stigma and financial hardship still hinder timely support.
Speakers urged stronger coordination among government, NGOs and partners, expansion of therapy and inclusive education, better referral pathways, digital screening, improved data management and a larger skilled workforce. They emphasized accessible, family‑centred services, greater public awareness and sustained investment in community‑based rehabilitation.
The policy brief recommended integrating disability screening into primary healthcare, strengthening referrals, expanding rehabilitation, supporting caregivers, promoting inclusive education and ensuring sustainable financing.
“Early identification and intervention are critical to ensuring that children and youth with disabilities reach their full potential. While Bangladesh has made significant progress in reducing child mortality, greater attention is needed to developmental support during the first 1,000 days of a child’s life and beyond. Strengthening referral pathways, expanding access to health, education and social services, and supporting families with timely information and care can make a lasting difference. Children in climate-vulnerable and geographically isolated areas deserve equal opportunities, and coordinated action across government, communities and service providers is essential to ensure inclusive development for all.”
“Investing in early identification and intervention for children with developmental delays and disabilities is not only a social responsibility but also an economic necessity. Evidence shows that timely intervention significantly improves children’s development and reduces long-term costs for families and the state. Many children in rural and underserved areas still lack access to screening and support services, while misconceptions often delay treatment and care. Strengthening referral systems, expanding access to services, and raising awareness among families are crucial. The experiences gathered from communities highlight the need for coordinated action so that every child can reach their full potential and contribute meaningfully to society.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical to improving outcomes for children with disabilities, particularly in underserved communities. Through this project, we identified around 1,500 children in two vulnerable upazilas and connected them with screening, rehabilitation, referral, nutrition and assistive device supports. We also worked with caregivers, teachers and local communities to reduce stigma and strengthen inclusive education. Our experience shows that coordinated action across health, education and social protection sectors can significantly improve access to services and ensure that children with disabilities receive the support they need to develop, learn and participate fully in society.”
“Early identification and intervention for children with disabilities and developmental delays reduces long-term public costs. A recent project end learning assessment in the coastal sub-districts of Banshkhali, Chattogram, and Patharghata, Barguna, proves that community-led initiatives, including caregiver involvement, home visits by community interns, and stronger referral lines, greatly improve access to vital services in these remote areas. Despite this progress, social stigma and a lack of specialist care remain significant barriers. Moving forward, the key to leaving no child behind lies in embedding early identification directly into public systems and strengthening community-based support.”
“When my daughter was five, she could neither walk properly, feed herself, nor respond when called. We had consulted many doctors but saw little improvement. Through community outreach support under the EIEI project, we received guidance, home-based exercises, nutritional support, and referrals. Gradually, she began walking, eating on her own, and interacting with others. Most importantly, she is now attending school alongside other children. This support transformed not only my daughter’s life but also our family’s future. Every child with a disability deserves the same opportunity, care, and chance to reach their potential.”
“As a woman with a physical disability, working as a community intern in a remote coastal area was never easy. Yet over 18 months, I witnessed remarkable transformations children once confined to beds began walking, speaking, and attending school. The greatest barrier was not disability itself, but stigma and lack of awareness. When families received support, guidance, and hope, they embraced inclusion. My experience proves that with timely intervention and community support, every child can thrive, and no disability should stand in the way of dignity, education, or opportunity.”
“Our field experience clearly shows that many disabilities could be prevented or mitigated through early identification and timely intervention. Families travel long distances seeking support because specialized rehabilitation services remain scarce at the community level. What stood out most was the overwhelming demand for care and the transformative impact of awareness, screening, and referral services. Disability should not remain a peripheral issue in development planning. Greater investment, stronger government support, and scaling up community-based interventions are essential to ensure that children with disabilities receive the care, inclusion, and opportunities they deserve.”
“My own life demonstrates why early identification and intervention matter. A vision impairment caused at age two was not diagnosed until I was six and treated only at 11—after critical developmental years had passed. In contrast, my niece’s eye condition was detected early and successfully managed, preventing lifelong disability. This project shows that timely screening, strong referral pathways, and coordinated action among health, education, and social protection services can significantly reduce functional limitations, improve inclusion, and help children with disabilities reach their full potential.”
“Early identification is the foundation of disability inclusion. If developmental delays and impairments are detected and addressed on time, many children can avoid lifelong disabilities and achieve their full potential. Technology can play a transformative role in accelerating screening and referrals, while disability corners at upazila health complexes can bring services closer to families. However, medical care alone is not enough. Strong collaboration among government agencies, NGOs, social services, and communities is essential to ensure rehabilitation, assistive devices, education, and inclusion. Investing in early intervention today will reduce disability burdens tomorrow.”
“Early identification is not simply about registering children in a database; it is about assessing their needs and ensuring timely intervention. Bangladesh has made remarkable progress in reducing child mortality, but many children who survive still face developmental disabilities and remain underserved. Sustainable progress requires coordinated action among health, social welfare and disability services. Community clinics, health complexes and disability support centres must work as one system. Without strong institutional linkages and continuity of care, gains made through short-term projects risk being lost, leaving vulnerable children behind.”
“Early identification is critical because the first years of a child’s life determine long-term development outcomes. Many children with developmental delays remain undetected due to limited screening tools and weak referral systems at the community level. Bangladesh needs a simple, nationally standardized early screening tool and stronger implementation at union and Upazila levels. Expanding field-level services, increasing trained personnel, updating disability data, and ensuring follow-up on policy recommendations can significantly improve access to support. Early intervention is not only a child rights issue it is an investment in the nation’s future.”
“Early identification and intervention require strong coordination among health, social welfare, education and disability service agencies. While NGOs have demonstrated effective community-based models, scaling them nationwide is the government’s responsibility. Investing in trained community health workers, strengthening doorstep services, engaging caregivers, and expanding local support systems can significantly improve outcomes for children with disabilities. A unified national database linked to birth registration would enable more efficient and inclusive service delivery.”
“Bangladesh has made significant progress in advancing the rights of persons with disabilities, from ensuring participation in BCS examinations to introducing Braille textbooks and enacting the Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act. However, implementation remains the key challenge. Stronger coordination across ministries, reforms in the Rules of Business, and active national committees are essential to ensure inclusive services. Persons with disabilities must be involved in planning and decision-making processes, while education, social protection and support services need greater monitoring and investment so that no one is left behind.”
“Early identification is the first and most important step in ensuring that children with disabilities receive the support they need to reach their full potential. Bangladesh has made significant progress in disability inclusion through laws, institutions and service centres, but challenges remain in expanding quality services and skilled human resources at the grassroots level. The government is working to strengthen rehabilitation and training facilities across the country, while continued collaboration between government agencies, NGOs and development partners will be essential to build a more inclusive society and improve the lives of persons with disabilities.”
“Early identification and intervention are not optional programmes they are a moral obligation. When children with disabilities receive support early, they have a greater chance to develop, participate and thrive. Families also benefit through reduced stress, improved wellbeing and stronger parent-child relationships. Yet too many children are identified too late and too many families continue to face stigma, isolation and a lack of information. Early intervention is not only the right thing to do; it is also one of the smartest investments a country can make. So early identification and early intervention need to be accessible, affordable and family centred. By acting early, we strengthen children, empower families and build a more inclusive and compassionate society.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical not only for children with disabilities but for every child’s development. When challenges are detected early and the right support is provided, children can reach their full potential, families face fewer burdens, and society benefits as a whole. Inclusive education is not merely an education issue it reflects the values of a civilized and developed nation. Strengthening inter-ministerial coordination, improving referral systems, and promoting behavioral change are essential to ensuring that no child is left behind and that every child has an equal opportunity to thrive.”
“Early identification and intervention are essential for helping children with developmental delays and disabilities reach their full potential. Yet many families face barriers due to limited information, delayed diagnosis and inadequate access to specialist services. My own experience as a parent showed how critical timely intervention can be. Bangladesh needs stronger data systems, more trained professionals, better referral pathways and accessible information in Bangla. This is not the responsibility of one institution alone; it requires coordinated action across government, communities and families to ensure that no child is left behind.”
“Early identification and intervention are critical for ensuring that children with disabilities reach their full potential. We need stronger coordination among government agencies, NGOs, health services and educational institutions to build an effective support system. The government is already in a process of expanding disability service centres, mobile therapy services and inclusive education initiatives, but more work remains. Reliable data, trained professionals, caregiver support and greater public awareness are essential to closing existing gaps. We must also strengthen referral pathways and community-based rehabilitation services. This is a long-term commitment that requires collective action, and we remain dedicated to building a more inclusive and accessible future for every child in Bangladesh.”
“Over the past three decades, we have worked to identify the needs of persons with disabilities, test solutions on the ground, and help integrate successful models into government systems. Bangladesh has made notable progress in inclusive education and rehabilitation services, but early identification and intervention must now become a national priority. The earlier a child is identified, the greater the opportunity for development and inclusion.”

item.title: Bangladesh trapped in the cheap clothes tag
item.description:
Bangladesh has retained its position as the world’s second-largest garment exporter, but the global apparel industry’s post-pandemic recovery is exposing a deeper weakness: while competitors move into higher-value products and capture new demand, Bangladesh remains trapped in the image of a low-cost manufacturing hub.
Although global apparel trade expanded by 4.46% to $574.46 billion in 2025-26, Bangladesh’s ready-made garment exports grew by just 0.89%, far behind Vietnam’s 10.53% and Cambodia’s 16.88%, according to industry data.
Manufacturers, economists and exporters say the sluggish performance reflects more than temporary challenges such as gas shortages, high borrowing costs or supply disruptions.
They argue the industry is confronting a structural problem that has become increasingly difficult to overcome: international buyers continue to associate Bangladesh with low-cost, high-volume production and remain reluctant to pay premium prices for complex, high-value garments.
As a result, factories that invest in technical apparel, functional clothing and sophisticated manufacturing often find themselves negotiating against the same low-price expectations attached to basic T-shirts and knitwear.
“International buyers still operate under the assumption that Bangladesh means cheap production,” said Mostafiz Uddin, founder and chief executive of Bangladesh Apparel Exchange.
“They push us for price cuts on complex items while willingly paying higher prices to other sourcing destinations for identical products. Competing solely on price is no longer a viable strategy.”
Industry leaders say the problem is compounded by destructive competition among local manufacturers, many of whom undercut one another to secure orders.
A senior BGMEA official said buyers sometimes offer as little as $5 for heavy winter jackets, prices that barely cover production costs.
“Factories accept orders with little or no profit just to keep production lines running,” the official said.
“That leaves almost nothing to invest in technology, product development or sustainability.”
Economists warn that Bangladesh is also losing competitiveness because it remains heavily dependent on imported synthetic fabrics, chemicals and specialised raw materials, lengthening production lead times at a time when global fashion brands increasingly prioritise speed over labour costs.
“The global apparel market has fundamentally changed,” said Fahmida Khatun, executive director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue.
“Cost is no longer the only deciding factor. Buyers increasingly demand faster delivery, digital traceability, carbon compliance and supply chain transparency. Bangladesh cannot compete effectively without strengthening its backward linkage industries.”
Khondaker Golam Moazzem, research director at CPD, said blaming weak export growth solely on external conditions ignores longstanding structural weaknesses.
“To shed the ‘cheap labour’ image, Bangladesh must invest aggressively in technical textiles, synthetic fibres, automation and innovation,” he said.
“Remaining dependent on basic cut-and-make production leaves the industry vulnerable to more integrated competitors.”
Analysts say escaping the low-cost trap will require a coordinated shift in industrial policy, including investment in synthetic fibre production, advanced textile manufacturing, automation and green technology, alongside efforts to build long-term partnerships with international brands rather than competing through relentless price cuts.
Without that transition, they warn, Bangladesh risks remaining the world’s second-largest garment exporter by volume while steadily losing ground in the industry’s fastest-growing and most profitable segments.

World football’s governing body FIFA vowed on Friday to press ahead with an “open and democratic” consultation on a proposed private investment plan despite widespread opposition to the proposal.

That opposition included a pledge by Europe’s governing body UEFA to boycott the World Cup if FIFA went ahead with its private investor plan.

FIFA said in a statement all of its member associations should have a chance to consider the plan.

“Nobody is selling football,” it said.

“This is not something FIFA would ever entertain.”

It also said it had heard feedback from UEFA and CONCACAF, the governing body for football in North and Central America, which said all 41 of its member associations had rejected FIFA’s proposal to sell a stake in the business operations of the World Cup.

The world body also said its planned consultation process had been “disrupted by incorrect media reports”.

“We respect the feedback and concern aired in public and reaffirm our commitment to an open and democratic consultation,” FIFA’s statement said.

“We will proceed with this consultation process to ensure that each (member association) has the ability to express its vote based on facts,” it said.

FIFA has said the plan it announced on Tuesday could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the commercial subsidiary it proposed to run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

If approved, the project could provide each of FIFA’s 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027 and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8.0 million to $20 million.

Private investors would be allowed under the proposal to acquire stakes in the company but would remain minority shareholders.

‘Never again’

UEFA said in an earlier statement none of its national teams would participate in any FIFA competition “for so long as these proposals remain alive”.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale,” it said.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino described the initiative on Wednesday as a “golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally”.

However, UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, who boycotted the World Cup final to show unhappiness with FIFA, said there was no place in world football for such a model.

“Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return,” he said.

“Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns. Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.”

Several leading European federations and European Union officials also criticised the proposal as another step in the commercialisation of sport, while also raising concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

The EU praised UEFA on Thursday for “defending the integrity of the game”.

“Proud to see Europe’s football associations leading on governance, standing firm on their principles,” European commissioner for sports Glenn Micallef said in a social media post.

CONCACAF members, including the three co-hosts of the recent World Cup, unanimously rejected the proposal on Thursday.

It said “the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies”.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has also expressed concern that the FIFA proposal was made public before all 211 member associations were fully consulted.

The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has also urged its members to review FIFA’s divisive plan.

‘Never for sale’

UEFA said in its statement on Thursday that the World Cup was “one of football’s greatest sporting legacies” and described the proposal as “a failure of leadership” and “governance by intimidation”.

“It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game,” UEFA said.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum—accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences.

“Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

item.title: Govt promises gazette publication for 3 BCS batches after verification by August
item.description:
The publication of gazettes for the 45th, 46th and 49th Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examinations remains pending despite the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (PSC) having issued its final recommendations.

Although considerable time has passed since the PSC completed the recruitment process, recommended candidates have yet to receive their final appointments.

The primary reason for the delay has been the slow pace of police verification. As the process has remained pending for an extended period, frustration and uncertainty among successful candidates have intensified. The government, however, is working to complete all verification procedures and publish the final gazettes by August.

State minister for Public Administration Abdul Bari recently confirmed the matter. He said all relevant agencies and departments are working intensively to complete the verification process as quickly as possible.

Delay in gazettes for 45th, 49th may leave 47th BCS posts vacant

According to him, all verification work is expected to be completed by August, assuring candidates that their prolonged and difficult wait will not continue much longer.

Candidates face financial and personal hardship

Under the normal recruitment process, verification begins after the PSC’s recommendation documents reach the Ministry of Public Administration. The ministry then forwards the files to the Special Branch (SB) of Police for verification.

However, delays in collecting field-level information and a lack of coordination among the agencies involved have significantly slowed the process. The administrative delays have had a direct and adverse impact on the lives of the recommended candidates.

At present, 1,807 candidates recommended under the 45th General BCS and 668 candidates under the 49th Special BCS are awaiting publication of the final gazette. The appointment process for 1,457 candidates recommended under the 46th BCS has also stalled in the same way.

After their names appeared on the PSC’s final list, the candidates and their families naturally celebrated the achievement. Many resigned from private-sector jobs, part-time employment or private tutoring—their primary source of income—in anticipation of joining government service.

However, the unusually long delay in gazette publication has exhausted their savings, leaving many of them in severe financial and personal hardship. Although they enjoy the social recognition of being known as future “BCS cadres” among relatives and friends, many are struggling to make ends meet.

PSC accelerates BCS process with ‘one year’ goal

Hundreds of posts in the 47th BCS may remain vacant

The delay in issuing appointment gazettes is also expected to affect the 47th BCS recruitment process.

Because appointments under the 45th, 46th and 49th BCS examinations remain pending despite final recommendations, many candidates have been compelled to sit for subsequent BCS examinations.

As a result, the same candidates are appearing on the merit lists of multiple BCS batches. If they eventually join under an earlier BCS, posts allocated under the 47th BCS could remain vacant. Those vacancies cannot be filled later, creating the risk that hundreds of valuable positions under the 47th BCS will go unfilled.

The situation could affect the overall functioning of the public administration. On the one hand, important government posts may remain vacant; on the other, thousands of new job seekers could lose opportunities.

Following the state minister’s assurance, affected candidates say they now want to see swift implementation. They have urged the government to publish the gazettes without delay and end the uncertainty surrounding their appointments.

item.title: Gas shortage adds to load-shedding misery
item.description:
A sharp nationwide gas shortage has persisted for more than a week following a reduction in the supply of liquefied natural gas (LNG). The shortage has disrupted industrial production and household cooking, while electricity generation has also fallen.

As a result, consumers are now facing widespread load-shedding in addition to the gas crisis. Daily power shortages have exceeded 2,500 megawatts. It remains uncertain when gas supply will return to normal.

According to sources at the Energy and Mineral Resources Division, Excelerate Energy has requested until 10 August to fully restore operations at its fire-damaged LNG terminal.

Before then, efforts are underway to restart the terminal’s undamaged boiler. If that unit can be brought back online, it will increase gas supply by 300 million cubic feet per day, easing the crisis to some extent.

Two Petrobangla officials told Prothom Alo that several replacement parts have already been imported from abroad and delivered to the terminal. Alongside the foreign technical team, engineers from a local shipbuilding company have joined the repair work.

Intensive efforts are underway to resume gas supply through the undamaged boiler as quickly as possible. However, officials are still unable to specify when it will become operational. A clearer picture is expected today or tomorrow (Friday or Saturday).

The government has also sought Malaysia’s assistance in addressing the gas crisis. Discussions are underway on importing LNG in ISO tank containers (specialised containers). Officials involved in the process said this is an expensive and time-consuming option, offering little prospect of immediate relief. They added that the gas shortage is unlikely to ease until the LNG terminal resumes operations.

The government has repeatedly expressed regret over the situation in recent days. Petrobangla and Titas Gas, the gas distribution company serving Dhaka, have also apologised to customers through public statements.

In another notice issued yesterday (Thursday), Titas said all categories of consumers in its service area would continue to experience severe low gas pressure until the situation improves.

Amid the severe gas shortage, Petrobangla has recently sought policy approval from the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources to propose higher gas prices for the power generation and CNG sectors.

It has proposed increasing gas prices by 67 per cent for electricity generation and 51 per cent for compressed natural gas (CNG) used in transport. It has also proposed raising distribution charges for the country’s six gas distribution companies.

If approved by the Energy Division, Petrobangla will submit a formal application to the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC). The regulator will then hold public hearings before making a decision.

However, Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Iqbal Hassan Mahmood told Prothom Alo yesterday that the government has no plans at present to raise gas prices.

He said people are already suffering from the gas shortage, which was triggered by a technical accident at one LNG terminal. Therefore, the government’s priority is to restore gas supply as quickly as possible to provide relief.

He added that work is also underway on long-term plans to diversify gas supply sources. He said he was not aware of any letter proposing a gas price increase.

Bangladesh imports LNG through two floating storage and regasification terminals (FSRUs) located off Maheshkhali in Cox’s Bazar. One is operated by the US company Excelerate Energy, while the other is operated by the private company Summit.

Gas supply from Excelerate’s terminal was suspended after a fire broke out there on 21 July, worsening the country’s gas shortage.

Consumers’ hardship continues

Around 35 to 40 per cent of Bangladesh’s daily gas supply normally comes from imported LNG. LNG imports can supply up to 1.05 billion cubic feet of gas per day, but yesterday that fell to 460 million cubic feet.

As a result, total daily gas supply has now dropped below 2.11 billion cubic feet, compared with estimated daily demand of 3.8 billion cubic feet. Before the terminal shutdown, around 2.7 billion cubic feet of gas was being supplied daily, which had kept the situation relatively stable.

Residents in different parts of Dhaka say they are unable to cook because of the shortage. Complaints have been particularly widespread in Mohammadpur and Adabor areas.

Jesmin Akter of Mohammadpur told Prothom Alo that after failing to get gas during the day, she waited from midnight until 3:00 am but still there was no gas flow. She said, in most of the houses in the Nobodoy Housing area there was no gas for the past two weeks.

Sumaiya Khan said she could not use gas for cooking for several days. Salma Akter said residents of Tajmahal Road have been unable to light their stoves even once over the past five days.

An official at the Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) said the further decline in gas supply has intensified public suffering. Many households are switching to electric stoves for cooking, increasing electricity demand.

Daily rainfall has helped keep demand somewhat under control, he said, otherwise load-shedding would have been even worse.

The situation is being managed by generating electricity from more expensive oil-fired power plants. He added that if gas prices for the power sector are increased, it will become difficult for BPDB to remain financially viable.

According to BPDB, gas supply to the power sector has fallen by more than 200 million cubic feet per day, reducing electricity generation by more than 1,500 megawatts.

Peak load-shedding exceeded 2,500 megawatts on Wednesday. During daylight hours yesterday, load-shedding still reached 2,330 megawatts. Power cuts have been more severe outside Dhaka, particularly in rural areas.

Industrialists say most factories in Narayanganj, Gazipur, and Valuka are receiving little or no gas pressure. Some factories have suspended production altogether, while others are operating at only 50 to 70 per cent of capacity.

In addition to gas shortages, factories have also been hit by load-shedding over the past several days. Some are using diesel generators as an alternative, while others are turning to renewable energy for electricity generation.

Petrobangla seeks to reduce financial deficit

According to Petrobangla sources, the company has had to purchase LNG at nearly double its previous price for the past four months since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East. As a result, it incurred losses of Tk 178.56 billion in the 2025–26 fiscal year.

The government has provided Tk 146 billion in subsidies, but Petrobangla still faces a deficit of Tk 32.56 billion. The company has continued to incur losses during July as global LNG prices remain elevated.

A senior Petrobangla official told Prothom Alo that before the conflict, LNG cost an average of USD 11 per unit. If LNG could again be purchased at that price, the proposed gas price increases would generate an additional Tk 85 billion in revenue for Petrobangla.

Part of that income would be used to cover higher distribution charges. If the proposed increase is still implemented, Petrobangla would no longer require subsidies. If subsidies were still necessary, they would amount to no more than Tk 15 billion, the official said.

However, sector insiders caution that global LNG prices may not return to previous levels anytime soon. Instability in the Middle East is worsening, and there are concerns that conflict could spread further, driving LNG prices even higher.

LNG currently trades at more than USD 21 per unit on the international market. As a result, the government may still need to provide subsidies even if gas prices are increased.

Industrial and residential consumers point out that industrial users must pay a fixed minimum monthly gas bill, while residential customers without prepaid meters are charged fixed monthly fees.

They are required to pay these bills even when they receive no gas supply. Yet Petrobangla seeks to raise prices whenever possible, they say. During the interim government’s tenure, gas prices for industry were increased by 33 per cent.

Before that, in 2023, the Awami League government raised average gas prices by 82 per cent, citing plans to improve supply. Industrial tariffs increased by as much as 178 per cent, but gas supply did not improve.

Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), told Prothom Alo that people have suffered from electricity and gas shortages for years, with the situation worsening several times annually for different reasons. Those who can afford it are switching to alternatives such as electric stoves and generators, he said.

The government, however, must take responsibility for protecting low-income households. He described Petrobangla’s proposal to raise gas prices during the current crisis as anti-consumer, arguing that the government should instead provide rebates on gas bills to customers who are not receiving gas supply.

item.title: Three of EU's 15 largest wildfires since 2016 occurred in July
item.description:
GREECE-ENVIRONMENT-CLIMATE-WEATHER-FIRE

Three wildfires that broke out within days of each other in Spain and France this month are among the 15 largest recorded in the European Union since 2016.

The largest wildfire in Spain's recent history broke out in the province of Avila, west of Madrid, on 22 July.

The blaze, which is still burning, has already scorched almost 44,000 hectares (109,000 acres), according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), making it the sixth-largest wildfire recorded in the EU over the past decade.

Major wildfire stabilises in central Spain but rising temperatures bring new alerts

A wildfire that broke out in the Guadalajara province, east of Madrid, is now the 14th-largest recorded in the EU since 2016, with more than 33,000 hectares burned.

France also entered the record books this month, with the country's largest wildfire since 1949 burning near Bordeaux since 22 July, although it is now considered to be "stabilised".

The blaze is the eighth-largest fire in the EU over the last 10 years, having destroyed more than 38,000 hectares (94,000 acres), according to EFFIS, which relies on satellite imagery analysis.

10,000 evacuated as France battles raging wildfires, Macron requests EU support

EFFIS figures may diverge from national data due to methodological differences, and estimates are updated as new satellite imagery becomes available.

A wildfire in Greece's Evros region in 2023 remains the largest recorded by EFFIS in the EU since 2016, having burned more than 96,000 hectares.

The next three largest fires all occurred in Portugal, in 2017 and 2025.

With around 91,000 hectares burned between the start of the year and the end of July, France has recorded its highest annual burned area since EFFIS records began in 2006.

Climate change fuelled conditions for Chile, Argentina wildfires: scientists

In Spain, the burned area so far this year is five times higher than the average for the same date over the previous 20 years.

The country is approaching, but has not yet exceeded, the highest cumulative area burned by the end of July on record.

Overall, the long-term average burned area has been exceeded in around 15 EU countries, including Germany, Italy, Portugal and Belgium.

item.title: India upper house approves tougher exam leak bill
item.description:
INDIA-GEN Z/

India’s upper house of parliament on Thursday passed a bill that would increase penalties for leaking exam papers following youth-led protests that demanded sweeping reforms and forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.

The legislation would double the maximum jail term for those involved in leaking exam papers to 10 years, and raise the maximum fine to more than $1 million.

Lawmakers approved it by a voice vote after several hours of discussion, a day after the lower house also passed the same bill.

“This is an issue in which every parent, every family, and indeed every citizen of this country has a stake, because these young children are our greatest investment,” Jitendra Singh, a junior minister who has negotiated with the protesters, told the Rajya Sabha, India’s upper house of parliament.

Protests rock India over medical entrance exam transparency

The bill must now be signed into law by President Droupadi Murmu.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s cabinet greenlighted the stricter punishments last week.

The approval followed weeks of mass protests over leaked exam papers and other irregularities, which culminated in the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday.

The protests, spearheaded by the online Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, drew massive support from students across the country and presented a major challenge to Modi’s government.

Despite repeated government crackdowns, leaks have remained a recurring problem in both national and state-level examinations.

On Tuesday, according to local media, India’s federal investigative agency charged 13 people with a range of crimes relating to the leak of a national medical college entrance test earlier this year—a controversy that helped fuel the youth protests.

Demonstrations against the paper leaks in New Delhi turned violent on 20 July when huge crowds attempted to march towards parliament.

Police fired tear gas and used batons to disperse the protest, triggering clashes and a wave of detentions.

item.title: Nepal PM urges calm after unrest leaves 3 dead
item.description:
TOPSHOT-NEPAL-POLITICS-VOTE

Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Thursday appealed for calm after clashes between Hindu and Muslim groups in the country’s south sparked unrest that has left three people dead.

Shah, who has kept a low profile since being elected in March, broke his silence to deliver his first address to the nation, calling on his countrymen to be “responsible citizens and remove the clouds of unrest”.

The violence began late Sunday in a village in the southern Sunsari district, which borders India, after an argument over loud music and the use of religious flags during a Hindu procession, according to officials.

Police opened fire to disperse the crowd, said local official Poshan Lamichhane. Two men died in the unrest, according to police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle.

Authorities are investigating the deaths and have imposed a curfew in Sunsari and neighbouring districts to prevent further clashes.

A third man was killed Thursday in the nearby Siraha district during a demonstration that took place while the curfew was in force.

“I, on behalf of the government, sincerely appeal to the citizens, civil society, religious communities, all respected leaders, all political parties and responsible media, to exercise patience and restrain and maintain peace, harmony, brotherhood and national unity,” Shah said in a video address.

Nepal, a secular republic where more than 80 percent of the population is Hindu, has seen tensions flare occasionally in the southern plains, where sizeable Hindu and Muslim communities live side by side.

In his address, Shah vowed that the investigation would be “completely fair and transparent”.

“The government is committed to bringing to justice whoever is responsible for the incident,” he said.

Kafle, the police official, said efforts were being made to restore order.

“We have kept all police officials in the field on alert and are trying to protect public property and prevent any conflicting situation with minimal use of force,” he told AFP.

item.title: Treating e-waste as an opportunity
item.description:
That Bangladesh generates an estimated three million metric tons of electronic waste annually, and that it recycles less than 10% of that waste through formal channels, is an extremely concerning reality for a nation that has aspirations of a more sustainable future.
That the majority of our e-waste ends up in informal scrapyards, landfills, and waterways, where toxic materials contaminate the soil and air, stand in sharp contradiction to our desire for a healthier country. It is safe to say that such negligence is no longer just an environmental concern but a public health and governance crisis.
The prevalence of informal recyclers dominating the sector, often working without protective gear while handling lead, mercury, cadmium, and other hazardous substances, also reflects poorly on the present state of affairs. Workers who are often below the age of 18 are frequently exposed to these toxins, with long‑term consequences for cognitive and physical development.
The other component to this failure is that Bangladesh is also losing economic value. E‑waste contains recoverable materials - copper, gold, and other rare earth elements - that could support a circular economy and create jobs, with reports stating that Bangladesh could recover over $200 million in resources annually through effective recycling.
Instead, these resources are being discarded or extracted unsafely, with no national system to capture their value.
The solution is clear, and it starts with recognizing recycling firstly as a moral imperative but also as a means to generate value. This means investing to build a nationwide collection network and modern recycling facilities while formalizing the informal sector with training and safety standards.
E‑waste is not garbage but an opportunity. Managed well, it can reduce pollution, recover valuable materials, and support our sustainable growth. Managed poorly, it will continue to be one of our most dangerous pollutants. The choice is clear.

item.title: Heat resilience must be a national priority
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest findings should alarm every policy-maker in Bangladesh: As per the the report, “A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities,” extreme heat cost our nation $18 billion in lost labour productivity and wiped out 465,000 jobs in Dhaka alone in 2024.
That this is projected to double in about 50 years is a reality we must prepare for from today itself, and do all we can to ensure that the worst does not come to pass.
What is most distressing about this is that it is hitting the poorest workers the hardest, thereby contributing to our widening inequality and undermining our development trajectory.
Our cities, especially Dhaka, have been trapped in a dangerous cycle of rising temperatures, expanding concrete, shrinking green spaces, and worsening air quality. The result has been all too predictable, with workers unable to continue or facing unbearable conditions to continue working.
To say Bangladesh must build heat‑resilient towns and cities is a gross understatement at this point. It is something we should have been planning for decades earlier.
However, given the exponential damage extreme heat does to our nation on a yearly basis, it is time to begin redesigning urban spaces with shade, ventilation, and greenery, enforcing building codes that reduce heat absorption, expanding our tree cover in our cities, and enact major reforms such as rethinking our transport infrastructure.
Better, more sustainable urban development is no longer optional but a survival strategy. Continuing to expand as a heat trap is not a solution, nor can it be classified as development. We must shift toward climate‑sensitive planning that prioritizes human health and economic resilience.
Extreme heat is already costing billions and destroying livelihoods. Without urgent action, the losses will continue to grow. We must treat heat resilience as a national priority. Our future depends on it.

item.title: Poison on our plates
item.description:
Food safety and environmental protection are inseparable pillars of sustainable development. A nation cannot claim genuine progress while its citizens are exposed to contaminated food and its natural environment continues to deteriorate.
Unfortunately, Bangladesh faces serious challenges in both areas, demanding stronger governance, institutional accountability, and unwavering political commitment.
Reports concerning food contamination have raised widespread public concern. Laboratory findings reportedly conducted by Professor Dr Abul Hossain of the Department of Chemistry, University of Dhaka, indicated elevated levels of chromium in broiler chicken meat, liver, brain, and commercial eggs. These findings have been attributed to the alleged use of chromium-contaminated tannery waste in poultry and fish feed, despite reported judicial restrictions on such practices.
Concerns have also been expressed regarding arsenic and other hazardous substances in farmed fish. If confirmed through independent scientific investigation, such contamination poses a serious threat to public health and demands immediate regulatory action.
When I joined the Bangladesh civil service, food adulteration was comparatively rare. Consumers generally had greater confidence in the quality of food, and ethical business practices were more widely respected.
Today, however, food adulteration has become a significant public health concern. Yet this problem is neither inevitable nor impossible to solve. It requires honest leadership, effective law enforcement, public awareness, and accountability at every level.
During my tenure as a Deputy Commissioner, I personally led campaigns against food adulteration, particularly during Ramadan, when the use of unauthorized colours and harmful chemical additives in iftar items was frequently reported. Regular mobile courts, market inspections, and coordinated enforcement by executive magistrates and law enforcement agencies significantly improved compliance.
Although some business leaders initially questioned these measures, I asked one of them a simple question: “Would you like your own children to consume adulterated food?” His answer was an immediate “No.”
That response reflected a universal truth -- every parent wants safe food for their family. Protecting public health should therefore unite, rather than divide, regulators and the business community.
Bangladesh also needs stronger environmental governance. Over the years, substantial public resources and international assistance have been invested in forestry, biodiversity conservation, and climate adaptation projects. While many initiatives have contributed positively, questions have also been raised regarding the effectiveness and transparency of certain projects.
Public investment should always be measured by tangible environmental outcomes -- such as increased forest cover, biodiversity conservation, pollution reduction, and climate resilience -- rather than by expenditure alone. Whenever credible allegations of irregularities arise, they should be investigated independently and impartially to strengthen public confidence.
The same principle applies to institutions responsible for environmental regulation and food safety. Their success should be judged by measurable improvements in environmental quality and consumer protection, not merely by administrative reports or completed projects. Strong institutions require transparency, professional competence, and accountability.
Although Bangladesh has enacted important legislation, including the Safe Food Act 2013, effective implementation remains the greatest challenge to its success.
Regulatory agencies must strengthen laboratory testing, surveillance, market inspections, and enforcement across the entire food supply chain. Equally important, officials who fail to discharge their statutory responsibilities through negligence or wilful inaction should, where legally appropriate, be held accountable.
Environmental crimes and deliberate food adulteration should not be treated as ordinary regulatory violations. They threaten human health, damage biodiversity, increase healthcare costs, and undermine sustainable development.
Consideration should therefore be given to strengthening penalties for serious offences, ensuring swift prosecution, and enhancing judicial capacity to deal with crimes that endanger public health and the environment.
Public awareness is equally essential. Governments, educational institutions, businesses, civil society, religious leaders, and the media all have a shared responsibility to promote a culture that values environmental stewardship and rejects food adulteration.
Sustainable progress cannot be achieved through laws alone; it depends on ethics, integrity, and collective responsibility.
Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to overcome major national challenges. There is every reason to believe that the country can also become a regional leader in food safety and environmental protection.
Achieving this goal, however, requires a genuine policy of zero tolerance toward food adulteration and environmental crimes, supported by strong institutions, transparent governance, scientific evidence, and the consistent application of the rule of law.
Protecting the environment and ensuring safe food are not merely administrative obligations -- they are moral responsibilities owed to every citizen.
Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is a former Additional Secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Bangladesh.

item.title: Dhaka air unhealthy for sensitive groups Friday morning
item.description:
The overcrowded capital Dhaka ranked 15th among cities with the worst air quality on Friday morning, recording an AQI score of 102 at 8:30am.
According to the AQI index, the city’s air was classified as “unhealthy for sensitive groups,” indicating potential health risks for vulnerable populations.
Uganda's Kampala, Kinshasa, capital and largest city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Indonesia's Jakarta topped the list with AQI scores of 187, 171, and 163, respectively.
An AQI between 50 and 100 is considered “moderate,” while 101 to 150 is deemed “unhealthy for sensitive groups.” Readings between 151 and 200 are classified as “unhealthy,” 201 to 300 as “very unhealthy,” and anything above 300 is regarded as “hazardous,” posing serious health risks.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is used to report daily air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and outlining possible health effects.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO₂), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution. Air quality typically worsens during winter and improves with the monsoon rains.
According to the World Health Organization, air pollution causes an estimated seven million deaths globally each year, largely due to stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.
